r.summary: The human evidence partly supports the Junior-dev idea, but the key causal step has not been tested. Three things are well supported. (1) Being made to explain a mechanism step by step lowers inflated confidence. This is the illusion of explanatory depth (Rozenblit & Keil 2002, replicated in preregistered studies). The effect is strongest for causal and mechanistic knowledge and absent for procedures. (2) Prompted explanation improves understanding (self-explanation meta-analysis, g = .55). (3) Experts are poor at predicting what novices will struggle with, and the bias resists debiasing (Hinds 1999). That argues for a separate, context-isolated novice over a "pretend you are a junior" prompt. Software inspection results back an outsider perspective with qualifications. Inspectors from outside computer science found more requirements defects (replicated), and ATAM risks are mostly omissions, meaning decisions never made, which is what novice questions are suited to surfacing. The counterevidence is substantial. Spontaneous novice questions are rare and mostly shallow, and shallow questions draw shallow "knowledge-telling" answers. Deep questions drew deep answers about three times as often (41% vs 14%). Reviewers unfamiliar with the code give superficial comments and catch "obvious bugs". Perspective-based reading shows no clear advantage in aggregate: it does worse than checklists, the perspectives do not find different defects, and there are signs of researcher bias. Explaining in writing to a fictitious student is not better than self-explaining. In the replications, recognizing ignorance did not change behaviour. Rubber-duck debugging rests on anecdote only, and Feynman-technique evidence is weak. Most importantly, nearly all of this evidence measures the explainer's learning or calibration, or a reviewer's defect detection. None of it tests whether explaining to a novice improves the explainer's design artifact, and none of it concerns LLMs. That is the core Junior-dev claim, and it has to be tested directly against strong baselines: self-explanation, a checklist reviewer, and matched token budgets.

findings.claim: Explaining a mechanism step by step exposes an illusion of understanding. Self-rated understanding drops sharply for devices and natural phenomena, much less for facts and narratives, and not at all for procedures.
findings.source: Rozenblit, L. & Keil, F. (2002). The misunderstood limits of folk science: an illusion of explanatory depth. Cognitive Science 26(5), 521-562 (12 studies).
findings.evidence: Abstract: "People feel they understand complex phenomena with far greater precision, coherence, and depth than they really do; they are subject to an illusion—an illusion of explanatory depth." Procedure: T1 rating, then a step-by-step written explanation and re-rating (T2), then a 'diagnostic' question and re-rating (T3), then an expert description and re-rating (T4). Table 1 gives Study 2 participants' self-ratings of 3.89 (T1), 3.10 (T2), 2.49 (T3) and 2.62 (T4) on a 7-point scale. In Study 1, the diagnostic question 'led to a further (non-significant) decrease.' Independent raters' judgments tracked the later, lower self-ratings. T1-T2 overconfidence: devices .918, natural phenomena .860, narratives .351, facts .291, procedures -.173. For procedures: "Instead of a drop in knowledge estimates we saw a slight (non-significant) increase." Samples were 12-54 per study, mostly Yale students. I read the first 100k of 157k characters on PMC.
findings.relevance: This is the central mechanism Junior-dev relies on: being made to explain how something works reveals gaps the explainer did not know about. It also limits the claim. The effect concerns causal and mechanistic content, which fits architectural logic, and does not appear for step lists. So questions should target how components interact, not what the steps are.

findings.claim: In preregistered replications, a mechanistic explanation reliably lowers self-rated understanding, but the effect is smaller than first reported and does not change downstream judgments. Giving reasons or justifications does not lower confidence and can entrench positions.
findings.source: Crawford, J.T. & Ruscio, J. (2021). Asking people to explain complex policies does not increase political moderation: three preregistered failures to closely replicate Fernbach et al. (2013). Psychological Science; and Fernbach, Rogers, Fox & Sloman (2013), Psychological Science.
findings.evidence: Crawford & Ruscio abstract: replications N = 306, 405 and 343. "Although participants reported less policy understanding after providing mechanistic policy explanations, policy-position extremity and in-group favoritism were unaffected." Mechanistic condition: understanding fell from 3.91 to 3.61 (1a) and from 3.88 to 3.62 (1b). Reasons condition: 3.85 to 3.86 (1a) and 3.95 to 4.10 (1b, an increase). "providing reasons increased extremity." The original effect on understanding was ηp² = .31; the replications gave .07 and .05. Fernbach 2013 abstract: the effects "did not occur when people were instead asked to enumerate reasons for their policy preferences."
findings.relevance: Questions that ask 'walk me through how X works' should expose gaps. Questions that ask 'why did you choose X' may only prompt justification and harden the plan. Noticing a gap also does not guarantee the explainer revises anything. Junior-dev assumes that revision step, and the human data does not show it.

findings.claim: Prompting people to explain improves understanding (meta-analytic g = .55). The benefit depends on accurate self-monitoring. Conceptual 'explain this' prompts beat metacognitive 'rate your understanding' prompts, and justification prompts are weaker.
findings.source: Chi, Bassok, Lewis, Reimann & Glaser (1989), Cognitive Science 13(2); Chi, de Leeuw, Chiu & LaVancher (1994), Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding, Cognitive Science 18(3); Bisra, Liu, Nesbit, Salimi & Winne (2018), Inducing self-explanation: a meta-analysis, Educational Psychology Review 30.
findings.evidence: Chi 1989: 'Good' students' explanations "are guided by accurate monitoring of their own understanding and misunderstanding"; 'Poor' students "do not generate sufficient self-explanations, monitor their learning inaccurately." Chi 1994: 14 prompted vs 10 control eighth-graders; "High explainers all achieved the correct mental model," but the prompted group spent about 1 hour longer (per Bisra). Bisra: 69 effect sizes, 64 reports, 5,917 participants, g = .55 [.45, .65]. Self-explanation beat instructional explanation (g = .35) and no added explanation (g = .67). Metacognitive prompts were not significant; conceptual prompts were more effective than metacognitive ones (z = 3.284, p = .001). Justify prompts g = .42. Self-explanation that took longer than the control gave g = .72, and equal-time studies gave .41 (difference not significant). Most studies did not report time on task.
findings.relevance: This supports asking the main agent to articulate the mechanism. It also says how to ask: content-specific 'explain how' prompts, not 'how confident are you'. Evaluations must control time or tokens, because uncontrolled time inflates explanation effects.

findings.claim: Explainers show a pervasive 'knowledge-telling' bias: they restate what they know instead of developing it. Learner questions can overcome this only when they are deep, and spontaneous learner questions are rare and mostly shallow.
findings.source: Roscoe, R.D. & Chi, M.T.H. (2007). Understanding tutor learning: knowledge-building and knowledge-telling in peer tutors' explanations and questions. Review of Educational Research 77(4), 534-574. It includes data from Roscoe & Chi (2004) and Graesser & Person (1994).
findings.evidence: Abstract: "peer tutors tend to exhibit a pervasive knowledge-telling bias. Peer tutors, even when trained, focus more on delivering knowledge rather than developing it." Roscoe & Chi 2004 data: tutees asked 152 shallow and 88 deep questions. "Only 14% of shallow questions received deep responses, whereas 41% of deep questions received deep responses. Similarly, 21% of shallow questions elicited self-monitoring, but 48% of deep questions prompted tutors to overtly evaluate their own thinking." The review adds that "tutee questions might indicate areas where tutors' knowledge is flawed" and that tutees may be confused "because the tutors' explanation is contradictory or incomplete." Graesser & Person 1994, as reported in this review (primary not read: the scan has no text layer): tutees asked 25 questions per hour, one third deep-reasoning, so "only 8 deep questions were asked in a typical session." The review suggests "simulated tutees could be programmed to ask only shallow questions or only deep questions."
findings.relevance: This is the most direct human evidence on the Junior-dev loop, novice questions acting on an explainer. Only deep questions (why, how, what-if, consequences) trigger the explainer's self-monitoring. A junior left to its own devices will ask shallow, definitional questions, and the main agent will answer by restating the plan.

findings.claim: Teaching that involves real interaction (answering questions) is associated with larger learning gains for the explainer than teaching without an audience. The interactive evidence base is small.
findings.source: Kobayashi, K. (2019). Interactivity: a potential determinant of learning by preparing to teach and teaching. Frontiers in Psychology 9:2755. A reanalysis of Kobayashi's 2018 meta-analysis.
findings.evidence: Table 2 (Hedges' g, random effects): indirect teaching (video or written, no interaction) after indirect expectancy, k = 12, g = 0.48 [0.43, 0.53]. Direct teaching with interaction after direct expectancy, k = 4, g = 0.84 [0.75, 0.93]. Direct vs indirect teaching expectancy: g = 0.50 vs 0.27. Conclusion: "a higher level of interactivity in expected and actual teaching substantially increases learning," with the caveat that "the currently available evidence, while still inadequate and subject to some exceptions." Also: "there is no single satisfactory explanation for why interactivity affects learning." Candidate mechanisms: questioning, information about the student, and motivation.
findings.relevance: This favours the interactive, question-driven design over a one-shot 'explain your plan to a novice' write-up. The outcome measured is the explainer's learning, not artifact quality, and the interactive cell has only k = 4.

findings.claim: Writing an explanation for a fictitious novice audience is no better, and sometimes worse, than self-explaining. Benefits from instructional explaining are small and mainly come from oral explaining.
findings.source: Lachner, A., Jacob, L. & Hoogerheide, V. (2021). Learning by writing explanations: is explaining to a fictitious student more effective than self-explaining? Learning and Instruction 74, 101438.
findings.evidence: Abstract (via Semantic Scholar): Experiment 1 (N = 147, lab, between-participants) found no effect of explaining. In Experiment 2 (N = 51, field, within-participants) only self-explaining beat the controls on transfer. "Self-explaining was more effective than instructional explaining." A cumulative meta-analysis found a small effect of instructional explaining, moderated by modality, with oral explaining more effective than written. A search snippet gave this effect as g = 0.22, which I did not confirm in the text I read.
findings.relevance: Junior-dev's explanations are written, and the novice audience is simulated. Any gain must therefore come from the questions and the forced revisions, not from framing the explanation for a junior. The key baseline is the main agent self-explaining its plan without a junior.

findings.claim: Experts predict novice difficulty worse than intermediates or novices do, and the bias resists debiasing. A separate novice perspective therefore adds information the expert cannot easily simulate.
findings.source: Hinds, P.J. (1999). The curse of expertise: the effects of expertise and debiasing methods on prediction of novice performance. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied 5(2), 205-221.
findings.evidence: Abstract (via OpenAlex): "In both studies, those with more expertise were worse predictors of novice performance times and were resistant to debiasing techniques intended to reduce underestimation. Findings from these studies suggest that experts may have a cognitive handicap that leads to underestimating the difficulty novices face and that those with an intermediate level of expertise may be more accurate in predicting novices' performance." Study 1 compared experts, intermediates and novices; Study 2 manipulated expertise experimentally.
findings.relevance: This justifies a context-isolated subagent over asking the main agent to 'imagine a junior'. It also suggests an 'intermediate' persona (technical, new to this stack) is a sound choice. It is human evidence about prediction, so its transfer to LLM self-simulation needs testing.

findings.claim: In modern code review, understanding the change is the main challenge, and clarification questions are the second most common comment type. Reviewers unfamiliar with the code mostly produce superficial comments and catch only obvious bugs, and few comments concern real defects.
findings.source: Bacchelli, A. & Bird, C. (2013). Expectations, outcomes, and challenges of modern code review. ICSE 2013, 712-721 (Microsoft).
findings.evidence: Methods: observation and interviews (17 interviewees), 570 comments in 200 threads, and surveys of 165 managers and 873 programmers. 'Code improvements' were 165 comments (29%); 'defect' was the fourth category at 78 (14%), and defect comments "mostly address 'micro' level and superficial concerns." Understanding was "the second most frequent category," covering "clarification questions and doubts." Interviewees said "if the code is not among their codebase, they look at 'obvious bugs (such as, exception handling).'" Of respondents, 798 (91%) said unfamiliar files take longer; 716 (82%) said familiar reviewers give different feedback, which is "substantially deeper, more detailed and insightful." "Developers indicated that when the author provided context and direction to them in a review, they could respond better and faster." Knowledge transfer was a motivation, but only 12 comments were explicitly about it.
findings.relevance: Clarification questions are a natural, frequent review outcome, which supports the Junior-dev interaction pattern. But a reader without context tends to find shallow issues, not deep design flaws. Expect Junior-dev to surface explanatory gaps and omissions, not stack-specific correctness errors.

findings.claim: Perspective-based reading, where reviewers take a stakeholder perspective and follow a scenario, helped in some original experiments, especially for less-experienced inspectors in unfamiliar domains. In aggregate it shows no clear advantage. It does worse than checklists, and the perspectives do not find different defects.
findings.source: Shull, Rus & Basili (2000), How perspective-based reading can improve requirements inspections, IEEE Computer; Fabbri, Maldonado, Shull, Carver, Basili et al. (2004), Data analysis of the first two PBR replications in Readers project, ICMC-USP TR-225; Regnell, Runeson & Thelin (2000), Empirical Software Engineering 5(4); Ciolkowski (2009), ESEM.
findings.evidence: Shull 2000 abstract: "PBR reviewers stand in for specific stakeholders... PBR leads to improved defect detection rates for both individual reviewers and review teams working with unfamiliar application domains." Fabbri TR, citing Shull: in familiar domains "experienced inspectors sometimes ignore the PBR procedure and use previously acquired heuristics... PBR may be better suited for less experienced inspectors." Its replications gave conflicting results across documents; individual PBR vs checklist p = .143 and .911 (R1), and .063 and .659 (R1+R2). Experience-effectiveness correlations were 'under 14%'. Perspective ANOVAs gave p = .654, .945 and .641. Regnell 2000 (N = 30): "there is no significant difference among the three perspectives in terms of defect detection rate." Ciolkowski 2009 abstract: "there is no clear positive effect of PBR: Inspection teams using PBR on requirements documents are more effective when compared to ad-hoc approaches, but are less effective when compared to checklists. In addition, we found strong indicators of researcher bias." The original Basili 1996 paper was read only through the TR's summary.
findings.relevance: PBR is the closest software analogue of 'review from a stakeholder's point of view'. Its record warns that a role persona alone is not reliably better than a plain checklist, and that adding more personas may not add coverage. Its strongest support is for structured, active tasks used by less experienced readers.

findings.claim: Requirements inspectors with degrees outside computer science found significantly more defects than CS graduates, and this replicated. Degree level and general industrial experience did not matter; experience writing requirements did.
findings.source: Carver, J.C., Nagappan, N. & Page, A. (2008). The impact of educational background on the effectiveness of requirements inspections: an empirical study. IEEE TSE 34(6). Replicated by Albayrak, O. & Carver, J.C. (2014), Empirical Software Engineering.
findings.evidence: Carver abstract (via OpenAlex): "a large-scale controlled inspection experiment with over 70 professionals was conducted at Microsoft... inspectors with university degrees in majors not related to computer science found significantly more defects than those with degrees in computer science majors... level of education (Masters, PhD), prior industrial experience or other job related experiences did not significantly impact the effectiveness... professionals with prior experience writing requirements found statistically significant more defects." Albayrak & Carver replication (Bilkent repository abstract): 69 professional developers at three Turkish companies; "inspectors whose degree is in a field related to software engineering are less effective"; results generally consistent.
findings.relevance: This is controlled, replicated evidence that a reviewer outside the specialist frame can find more defects in a specification. Familiarity with the artifact type (writing requirements) still helped. That supports a junior who knows how plans and diagrams work but not this stack.

findings.claim: In architecture evaluations (ATAM), most identified risks are omissions, meaning decisions or investigations never made, rather than bad decisions.
findings.source: Bass, L., Nord, R., Wood, W. & Zubrow, D. (2006). Risk Themes Discovered Through Architecture Evaluations. CMU/SEI-2006-TR-012.
findings.evidence: 18 ATAM evaluations produced 99 risk themes: "25 were risks of commission, 57 were risks of omission, and 17 were neither." Boeing's independent set: 16 omission, 11 commission, 1 neither (ratios 2.3:1 SEI, 1.5:1 Boeing). "the risk themes identify decisions or investigations that were never made rather than those that were made." Requirements-uncertainty themes were all omissions. The authors caution: "it's unclear whether a particular categorization of items is repeatable."
findings.relevance: If most architectural weaknesses are omissions, a questioner who keeps asking 'what happens when...' or 'who handles...' targets the main failure class. These risks were found by expert evaluators working with stakeholders, not by novices.

findings.claim: Expert practitioner guidance on design reviews says that uninformed reviewers turn reviews into tutorials and that passive reading misses unstated assumptions. It recommends reviews in which reviewers must use the document and answer open, specific questions instead of giving ok/not-ok verdicts.
findings.source: Parnas, D.L. (c. 2005-2006). Document Driven Testing and Inspection, lecture notes, University of Limerick. Summarizes Parnas & Weiss (1985), Active Design Reviews: Principles and Practices, ICSE.
findings.evidence: From 'Twelve Reasons Conventional Reviews are Ineffective': "(4) Reviewers can avoid potential embarrassment by saying nothing... (7) Presence of uninformed reviewers may turn the review into a tutorial... (11) Unstated assumptions are not questioned." Solutions: "Make the reviewers use the documents and document their analysis... Ask the reviewer about things they know. Make the reviewers provide specifics - not just a ok/not ok." Example questions: "Ask reviewers to identify 'error' cases. Ask reviewers to explain why no other error cases are possible." On Fagan inspections: "Read the code in sequence and paraphrase it in a natural language." The 1985 paper itself was not readable (DTIC blocked).
findings.relevance: This warns that a novice reviewer's default mode is a costly tutorial. It also gives a concrete fix: have the junior use the plan, for example by tracing scenarios, listing error cases and explaining why no others exist, rather than only asking about it.

findings.claim: How much interactive group rounds add beyond individual preparation is contested. In one industrial study, inspection meetings added few faults at high cost; other studies report larger meeting gains.
findings.source: Votta, L.G. (1993). Does every inspection need a meeting? ACM SIGSOFT FSE '93. The contrasting figure is from Porter, Siy, Toman & Votta (1997), IEEE TSE, reported secondarily.
findings.evidence: Votta abstract (via OpenAlex): "we have found that these inspection meetings are not as beneficial as managers and developers think they are. Even worse, they cost much more in terms of products development interval and developer's time than anyone realizes." Secondary sources from search, not the papers: about 5% meeting gain across 50 design inspections (Votta); a 33% average meeting gain with large variance across more than 100 AT&T code inspections (Porter et al.).
findings.relevance: Later Q&A rounds may yield little beyond the first. Junior-dev should measure what each round adds and stop early, not run rounds until the junior is satisfied.

findings.claim: Developers' hardest-to-satisfy information needs concern design rationale and intended behaviour. Onboarding studies document newcomers' questions and their hesitation to ask, but do not measure whether those questions improve mentors' artifacts.
findings.source: Ko, A.J., DeLine, R. & Venolia, G. (2007). Information needs in collocated software development teams. ICSE 2007. Ju, A., Sajnani, H., Kelly, S. & Herzig, K. (2021). A case study of onboarding in software teams: tasks and strategies. ICSE 2021 (arXiv 2103.05055).
findings.evidence: Ko abstract: 17 developers observed. "The most often deferred searches included knowledge about design and program behavior, such as why code was written a particular way, what a program was supposed to do, and the cause of a program state. Developers often had to defer tasks because the only source of knowledge was unavailable coworkers." Ju et al.: 32 developers and 15 managers interviewed at Microsoft; mentors matter because "new members can ask mentors 'dumb' questions freely"; some newcomers hesitate to ask; 90% of surveyed developers said complete, up-to-date documentation helps. The paper does not measure costs or benefits to mentors.
findings.relevance: This identifies which questions matter: rationale, intended behaviour and causes of state, which plans usually leave implicit. There is no software-team evidence that answering newcomer questions improves the answerer's design documents. That gap is exactly the Junior-dev hypothesis.

findings.claim: Rubber-duck debugging has no direct empirical test; its support is anecdote plus analogy to self-explanation. Evidence for the 'Feynman technique' is weak and conflated with learning-by-teaching.
findings.source: University of Sydney news article (2025-09-25), 'Stuck on a problem? Talking to a rubber duck might unlock the solution'; Dai et al. (2026), The impacts of the Feynman learning method on students' learning outcomes: a meta-analysis of 41 empirical studies, Advances in Education 16(9) (Hans); Rajesh & Khan (2025), Learn Like Feynman: an AI-driven Feynman Bot (arXiv, summary page).
findings.evidence: The Sydney article cites no direct study of rubber-duck debugging. It traces the term to an anecdote in The Pragmatic Programmer and argues by analogy from learning-by-teaching and self-explanation research. Feynman meta-analysis: 41 studies, 44 effect sizes, N = 4,071, g = 0.468 [0.379, 0.556]. Its search terms included 'learning by teaching'; 33 of 44 effect sizes measured declarative knowledge; Egger's test gave t = 1.968, p = 0.056; heterogeneity was high in university and STEM subgroups. Feynman Bot: 14 participants over three days against a 'Passive Learners' group, with no effect sizes reported.
findings.relevance: The folk techniques often cited for 'explain it to a novice' cannot carry the design rationale. Any justification has to rest on f1-f5 and on direct tests of Junior-dev.

design_implications: Write the junior's question templates to demand mechanism, not justification. Examples: 'Trace a request for X step by step through each component', 'What happens if Y times out, fails, or runs twice?', 'Where does state Z live and who changes it?'. Avoid leading with 'Why did you choose X?'; ask 'What would break if X were replaced?' instead. Mechanistic explanation is what exposes gaps (f1, f2). Justification prompts are weaker or entrench positions (f2, f3). Open, specific questions beat ok/not-ok verdicts (f12).

Explicitly steer the junior towards deep questions (causal, what-if, failure, consequence) and set a minimum share per batch. Left alone, novice questions are mostly shallow, and shallow questions draw restated answers (f4). Log each question's type (shallow/deep, mechanism/rationale/definition) so evaluations can check whether question depth predicts plan changes (f4, f14).

Do not use 'the junior says it understands' as the stopping rule; a fluent restated answer can satisfy it (f4). Require a teach-back instead. After each round, the junior writes its own trace of one or two concrete scenarios using only the plan and the answers, and the main agent marks where the trace differs from its intent. Each mismatch is a candidate plan edit. This puts into practice 'make reviewers use the document' (f12) and the diagnostic step that further lowered illusory confidence (f1).

Keep the junior context-isolated and do not replace it with a self-prompt like 'imagine explaining to a junior'. Experts mis-predict novice difficulty and resist debiasing (f7). Still include self-explanation as a baseline, because writing for a fictitious novice was no better than self-explaining (f6).

Make the persona an 'intermediate': fluent in software design and in reading plans and diagrams, unfamiliar with this stack. Do not make it a layperson. Intermediates predict novice difficulty best (f7); outsiders to the specialist frame find more specification defects, but familiarity with the artifact type helps (f10); structured perspective reading helps less-experienced readers most (f9).

Scope the claim to omissions, ambiguities and unstated assumptions, not stack-specific correctness. Unfamiliar reviewers catch shallow issues and 'obvious bugs' (f8). Most architectural risks are omissions (f11). Pair Junior-dev with a stack-aware or test-based check wherever correctness matters, and say so in the skill description.

Guard against filling the plan with confabulated detail. The junior cannot check answers because it has no repo access, and the main agent's default answer is knowledge-telling (f4). Have the main agent tag each answer claim as stated-in-plan, verified-in-repo, or assumption. Only verified claims, or claims explicitly marked as assumptions, go into the revised plan. Evaluation should score whether plan additions are correct, not just how long they are (f2: noticing ignorance did not change outcomes).

Run the evaluation on plans with seeded defects, following the inspection-experiment tradition (f9, f10). Seed several types: missing failure handling, missing state ownership, unstated assumptions, contradictory flows, and stack-specific API errors. Report detection rate and false-positive edits per type (f8, f11).

Use strong baselines at matched token and time budgets: (a) no review; (b) the main agent self-explains its plan step by step with no junior (f3, f6); (c) a checklist reviewer, which beat PBR in aggregate (f9); (d) optionally a critical reviewer. Junior-dev must beat (b) and (c), not just (a). Control tokens and time because uncontrolled time inflates explanation effects (f3).

Measure what each round adds: defects found, plan edits and teach-back mismatches per round. Cap rounds, and stop when a round produces no edit or mismatch. Interaction helps (f5), but the extra yield of further group rounds is contested and costly (f13), and uninformed reviewers drift into tutorials (f12).
Start with one well-designed junior persona before adding several stakeholder personas. PBR's perspectives did not find different defects in controlled tests (f9).

Primary outcome: downstream task success and defect counts when the revised plan is implemented. Secondary outcomes: seeded-defect detection, question-depth distribution and cost. The human literature mostly measures the explainer's calibration or learning (f1, f3, f5) and shows that recognizing a gap is not the same as fixing it (f2). Artifact improvement has to be measured directly.
open_questions: The causal chain from explaining to a novice, to finding gaps, to revising and improving the artifact has no direct human test. The literature shows lower self-assessed understanding (f1, f2), better explainer learning (f3, f5) and reviewer defect detection (f8-f10), but not better artifacts from the explainer. Junior-dev's core claim therefore has to be established by its own experiments.
Do LLMs have an analogue of the illusion of explanatory depth? Under questioning, does a model detect gaps, or does it confabulate plausible detail that makes the plan longer but not more correct?
Can an LLM playing a junior keep to a novice perspective even though it knows the stack? Without repo access, can it tell answers that close a gap from answers that just sound complete?

Do weaker main models (Haiku, Sonnet) benefit more, or less? The human evidence cuts both ways. Poor self-explainers monitor inaccurately (f3), yet prompting helps them. Chase et al. (2009, abstract only, not in the findings) report teachable-agent gains largest for lower-achieving students. No LLM data exists.
Is the collaborative, non-adversarial stance worth some loss of defect-finding power compared with a critical or checklist reviewer at the same budget? Checklists beat PBR in aggregate (f9).

What batch size and number of rounds work best, and does a teach-back trace find more gaps than question batches alone? Human evidence on extra rounds is contested (f13), and the interactive learning-by-teaching base is small (f5, k = 4).

Which plan defects can a question-only reader without context catch at all? The human data suggests omissions and ambiguities but not domain-specific incorrectness (f8, f11). This needs a defect-type breakdown on real plans and Mermaid diagrams.

Primary sources I could not open: Basili et al. 1996 (read through the Fabbri TR), Parnas & Weiss 1985 (read through Parnas's later lecture), Graesser & Person 1994 (read through Roscoe & Chi), and Fiorella & Mayer 2013/2014 and Kobayashi 2022 (abstracts seen only in search results). Their exact figures should be checked before any of them carries weight.

r.summary: No study tests Junior-dev's exact setup: a novice questioner that sees only an architectural plan or diagram and quizzes the agent that wrote it. The evidence below comes from nearby setups, mostly 2023-2026, and it supports a narrower version of the hypothesis than the one stated. (1) Refinement only helps when an external signal enters the loop. A model critiquing its own work, called intrinsic self-correction, does not improve reasoning and often makes it worse, and the weakest model tested got worse the most (Huang, ICLR 2024; Kamoi, TACL 2024). On plans specifically, a model checking plans approved 84% of invalid ones (Valmeekam). Self-Refine's roughly 20-point average gain is mostly on style and preference tasks: on math it adds 0.2 points, and its feedback said "everything looks good" for 94% of instances. (2) Questions do help when the person answering holds information the asker lacks. Clarification gives +7.7 to +8.7 pass@1 (ClarifyGPT) and up to +74% on an underspecified version of SWE-bench (Ambig-SWE). A separate agent whose job is to detect missing information beat a single agent that could ask (61.2% to 69.4% resolved with Sonnet 4.5). Short, targeted questions get answered far more accurately than the original long-form output (CoVe: about 70% vs 17%). In Junior-dev, though, the answerer is the plan's own author, so the setup is structurally "consultancy": one expert answers a non-expert who cannot check the ground truth. Under consultancy, LLM judges reached only 54%, against 48% with no expert at all, and the more skilled the consultant, the more easily wrong answers persuaded the judge (Khan, 2024). (3) The main risks are documented and large. Models wrongly admit mistakes or change answers when challenged (GPT-4 changed 32% of answers, Claude 1.3 changed 86%; flip-flop rate 46%). Their explanations can rationalize an answer rather than report why they gave it, with accuracy drops of up to 36%. Prompt-only novice personas leak expert knowledge and silently fill gaps, more so across many turns. Models find the single right missing piece only 40-50% of the time on planning tasks. (4) The claim that this especially helps weaker models is not supported, and the evidence leans the other way. Weaker models gain less from self-repair and explanation: Code Llama repaired 1.1% vs GPT-4's 10.8%, StarCoder gained 0 from explanation, and Vicuna-13B could not refine at all. Haiku 3.5 extracted as much information from clarification as Sonnet 3.5 but resolved 26.8% vs 39.6% of tasks, so the bottleneck is using the answers. Two things are plausible but untested for plans: a cheaper questioner (weak students helped strong teachers in Ning et al., NeurIPS 2024), and the benefit of hearing questions from another agent (models fail to correct 64.5% of errors they would catch if the same errors were attributed to someone else). Overall, the intent is sound only if every answer is grounded in the repo and checked, and Junior-dev's value must be measured against an external ground truth, not against the junior saying it understands.

findings.claim: Intrinsic self-correction does not reliably improve reasoning and often degrades it. Gains reported in earlier work depended on oracle labels or other external feedback. The weakest model tested degraded the most.
findings.source: Huang et al. 2023, 'Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet', ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2310.01798); corroborated by Kamoi et al. 2024, 'When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs', TACL vol. 12
findings.evidence: Huang Table 1, standard prompting to self-correct round 2. GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9->74.7, CommonSenseQA 75.8->41.8. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5->89.0, HotpotQA 49.0->43.0. Llama-2: GSM8K 62.0->36.5, CSQA 64.0->36.5. With oracle labels, GPT-3.5 CSQA rose 75.8->89.7. The paper says 'the improvements vanish when oracle labels are not available.' Kamoi's abstract: 'no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs', except on tasks unusually suited to it; self-correction works well 'with reliable external feedback'.
findings.relevance: Junior-dev is mostly intrinsic: the junior's questions are generated by an LLM, and the answers come from the plan's author. Without a source of truth outside the loop, the literature predicts little gain, with the largest harm on weaker main agents.

findings.claim: Self-Refine's large average gains come from preference and style tasks. On tasks with hidden correctness errors, the model's own feedback rarely finds anything to fix, and a weaker model could not run the loop at all.
findings.source: Madaan et al. 2023, 'Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback', NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv 2303.17651)
findings.evidence: The abstract reports '~20% absolute on average' improvement. Table 1, GPT-4: Dialogue Response 25.4->74.6, Code Readability 27.4->56.2, Code Optimization 27.3->36.0, Math Reasoning 92.9->93.1 (+0.2). On math, ChatGPT's feedback was 'everything looks good' for 94% of instances, and 'a consistent-looking reasoning chain can deceive LLMs'. Vicuna-13B 'was not able to consistently generate the feedback in the required format' and 'either repeated the same output or generated a hallucinated conversation.'
findings.relevance: Expect Junior-dev to make plans read more completely, a style gain, more readily than it makes them more correct. A plan that looks consistent may produce no questions about its real flaws.

findings.claim: On planning tasks, an LLM checking LLM-made plans approves most invalid ones. A sound external verifier more than doubles the improvement.
findings.source: Valmeekam, Marquez & Kambhampati 2023, 'Can Large Language Models Really Improve by Self-critiquing Their Own Plans?' (arXiv 2310.08118; no venue on the arXiv page)
findings.evidence: Blocksworld, GPT-4, 100 instances: LLM alone 40%; LLM+LLM self-critique with backprompting 55%; LLM plus the external VAL verifier 88%. The LLM verifier produced 38/45 false positives (84.45%), and the abstract says LLM verifiers 'produce a notable number of false positives, compromising the system's reliability.'
findings.relevance: This is the closest evidence to architectural plans. The junior, an LLM, deciding that it 'understands' the plan is a weak verifier and will likely accept flawed plans. Correctness has to be checked by something other than the junior's satisfaction.

findings.claim: Feedback quality limits refinement. Stronger-model or human feedback gives much larger gains, tool-grounded critique beats tool-free critique, and weaker code models benefit least from self-repair.
findings.source: Olausson et al. 2023, 'Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?', ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2306.09896); Gou et al. 2023, 'CRITIC' (arXiv 2305.11738)
findings.evidence: Olausson: 'substituting a weaker model's own feedback with that of a stronger model significantly improved performance.' Human feedback vs GPT-4 feedback on 40 failing GPT-4 programs: 52.60% vs 33.30% of repairs pass, '1.58x'. Overall APPS repair success: Code Llama 1.1%, GPT-3.5 4.7%, GPT-4 10.8%, and 'Code Llama benefits less'. CRITIC (ChatGPT), with tools vs without: AmbigNQ F1 74.9 vs 67.3, HotpotQA 52.9 vs 46.1, GSM8K 78.2 vs 77.0. The paper says relying on self-correction alone 'may yield modest improvements' or 'even deteriorate performance'.
findings.relevance: How good the questioner is, and whether answers are grounded in tools such as repo reads and commands, will decide whether Junior-dev works. A weak main agent answering from its own memory is the worst case.

findings.claim: Rubber-duck self-explanation of code helps little without execution feedback. Without execution, models stay overconfident in their first answer, and gains from explanation are inconsistent across models, with none for the weakest model tested.
findings.source: Chen, Lin, Schärli & Zhou 2023, 'Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug' (arXiv 2304.05128)
findings.evidence: Spider (no unit tests), baseline -> +explanation: Codex 81.3->84.1, GPT-3.5 71.1->72.2, GPT-4 73.2->73.6, StarCoder 64.7->64.9. On MBPP, adding explanation to unit-test feedback changed accuracy by +0.4 (Codex), +2.0 (GPT-3.5), -0.2 (GPT-4), 0 (StarCoder). Without execution, 'both models tend to be overconfident in their own initial predictions'. The paper concludes that 'code execution plays an important role in Self-Debugging.'
findings.relevance: This directly tests the idea that being forced to explain exposes errors. Explanation alone gives small, model-dependent gains, and for weaker models explanation by itself showed no reliable benefit.

findings.claim: Breaking an output into short, targeted questions improves accuracy because models answer narrow questions more accurately than they generate long-form content. Answering each question without the draft in view avoids repeating its errors. Socratic sub-questioning gives moderate gains at several times the inference cost.
findings.source: Dhuliawala et al. 2023, 'Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in LLMs' (arXiv 2309.11495); Qi et al. 2023, 'The Art of SOCRATIC QUESTIONING: Recursive Thinking with LLMs' (arXiv 2305.14999)
findings.evidence: CoVe: only about 17% of baseline-listed Wikidata entities were correct, but about 70% were answered correctly 'when querying each individual entity via a verification question'. Llama-65B list precision 0.17->0.36. Biography FactScore 55.9->71.4 (factor+revise). 'Verifying questions should not attend to the original baseline response as they may be prone to repeating it'; factored beat joint on all tasks. Qi (ChatGPT) average accuracy: standard 45.00, CoT 45.12, Socratic (2 turns) 50.51. This took 9.22 LLM calls per instance vs 1. The authors note 'self-checking functionality lacks sufficient sensitivity' and that overconfidence leads to few sub-questions.
findings.relevance: This is the strongest support for the question-driven idea. Narrow questions about specific steps are answerable, and answering them can reveal errors. But answers produced while the plan is in view tend to restate the plan.

findings.claim: LLMs are poor at finding the one missing piece of information in planning and logic problems, even when they can solve the fully specified version.
findings.source: Li, Kim & Wang 2025, 'QuestBench: Can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?', NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks (arXiv 2503.22674)
findings.evidence: Models do well on GSM-Q and GSME-Q but reach only '40-50% accuracy on Logic-Q and Planning-Q', and they 'struggle to identify the right question even when they can solve the fully specified version.'
findings.relevance: The junior's main job is to spot what is missing from a plan. On planning-like structure, expect it to find the real gap about half the time at best. Question coverage of known gaps should be a primary evaluation metric.

findings.claim: On underspecified SWE-bench tasks, interaction recovers most of the lost performance, and a separate agent that detects underspecification beats a single agent with an ask tool. Models almost never ask unless told to, and weaker models make worse use of the answers they get.
findings.source: Vijayvargiya et al. 2025, 'Ambig-SWE: Interactive Agents to Overcome Underspecificity in Software Engineering', ICLR 2026 (arXiv 2502.13069); Edwards & Schuster 2026, 'Ask or Assume? Uncertainty-Aware Clarification-Seeking in Coding Agents', EMNLP 2026 camera-ready per arXiv (arXiv 2603.26233)
findings.evidence: Ambig-SWE: interaction boosts performance on underspecified inputs by 'up to 74%'. 'Without explicit prompting, models almost never interact, even for severely underspecified inputs.' Share of full-spec performance recovered: Sonnet 4 89%, Sonnet 3.5 and Haiku 3.5 up to 80%, DeepSeek-v2 59%, Llama 3.1 70B 54%. Sonnet 3.5 and Haiku 3.5 extracted the same information (0.136 vs 0.135) but resolved 39.6% vs 26.8%: 'how models integrate information matters as much as how much they extract.' Ask or Assume, Sonnet 4.5: full 70.80, hidden 54.80, single agent with ask tool 61.20, multi-agent detector 69.40, at $3.50 vs $2.03 per task. The simulated user held the full issue (GPT-5.1).
findings.relevance: A separate questioning agent is supported. But the gains depend on the answerer holding the true information, a simulated user with the full spec, and on the model integrating answers. Haiku as main agent may answer well yet revise the plan poorly.

findings.claim: Detecting ambiguity, asking clarifying questions and then refining the requirement improves code generation by similar amounts for GPT-4 and ChatGPT.
findings.source: Mu et al. 2023, 'ClarifyGPT: Empowering LLM-based Code Generation with Intention Clarification' (arXiv 2310.10996; the arXiv page lists no venue)
findings.evidence: Human evaluation (10 participants, MBPP-sanitized): GPT-4 pass@1 70.96% -> 80.80%. Automated evaluation with simulated user responses across four benchmarks: GPT-4 68.02% -> 75.75%, ChatGPT 58.55% -> 67.22%. Ambiguity is first detected 'by performing a code consistency check'.
findings.relevance: This is positive evidence for the question-then-refine loop, and the weaker model gained as much as GPT-4. The answers come from the requirement's owner, who knows the true intent, and an objective trigger (inconsistent sampled code) decides when to ask.

findings.claim: When a non-expert who cannot see the ground truth questions a single expert ('consultancy'), the non-expert gains little accuracy and is more easily misled by an incorrect expert, especially a skilled one. Adversarial debate does much better.
findings.source: Khan et al. 2024, 'Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers' (arXiv 2402.06782); Kenton et al. 2024, 'On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs' (arXiv 2407.04622)
findings.evidence: Khan, judges without access to the story text. GPT-4-Turbo judges: naive 48%, consultancy 54%, debate 75.6% (expert judge 92.5%). Human judges: 60% / 78% / 88%. 'Higher consultant skill leads to worse accuracy'; 'In consultancy, incorrect experts cause low judge accuracy, suggesting that it is easier to be misled in consultancy.' Kenton: debate beat consultancy on every task when the consultant was randomly assigned to argue for the correct or incorrect answer, and judges were 'less frequently convinced by the wrong answer in debate than in consultancy.'
findings.relevance: Junior-dev is structurally consultancy. The junior sees only the plan and the author defends it. A fluent main agent can satisfy the junior with wrong answers, so the junior's 'I understand' is not evidence that the plan is correct.

findings.claim: Models frequently cave to challenges by wrongly admitting mistakes and flipping correct answers, which lowers accuracy across many models.
findings.source: Sharma et al. 2023, 'Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models' (arXiv 2310.13548); Laban et al. 2023, 'Are You Sure? Challenging LLMs Leads to Performance Drops in The FlipFlop Experiment' (arXiv 2311.08596)
findings.evidence: Sharma, after the challenge 'I don't think that's right. Are you sure?': models admit mistakes on 42% (GPT-4) to 98% (Claude 1.3) of questions and change their answer on 32% to 86%, with accuracy down by up to 27% for Claude 1.3. 'Swaying is not limited to answers the LM has low confidence in.' Laban, 10 LLMs on 7 tasks: models 'flip their answers on average 46% of the time', with 'an average drop of 17%' in accuracy.
findings.relevance: Junior questions can read as implicit challenges. The main agent may change correct parts of the plan to accommodate the junior, so plan changes need justification. Separately, the junior may accept a confident answer.

findings.claim: LLM explanations can be plausible yet unfaithful, rationalizing answers driven by factors the model never mentions.
findings.source: Turpin, Michael, Perez & Bowman 2023, 'Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting', NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv 2305.04388)
findings.evidence: Biasing features, such as reordering few-shot options so the answer is always '(A)', caused accuracy drops 'as much as 36%' across 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks (GPT-3.5, Claude 1.0). The explanations did not mention the bias and rationalized the biased answers, which the authors call 'plausible yet misleading'.
findings.relevance: Explaining a plan to a novice can produce confident, coherent but invented justifications for plan steps. This confabulation risk has to be controlled by grounding answers in the repo.

findings.claim: A novice persona set up by prompt alone leaks expert knowledge: simulated learners skip required reasoning steps and act more competent than assigned, more so in multi-turn dialogue.
findings.source: 'Too smart for its own good? Competence Leakage in LLM Simulations of Young Learners', NeurIPS 2026 (virtual abstract page); Song, Guo & Lin 2026, 'Simulating Novice Students Using Machine Unlearning and Relearning in LLMs' (arXiv 2603.26142)
findings.evidence: NeurIPS 2026 abstract: real traces showed over-competency dominated, with simulators dropping prescribed misconceptions or skipping required reasoning steps. The same trigger caused more leakage in multi-turn interaction than in isolation. Stronger models adhered better, but reasoning was associated with more leakage in multi-turn settings. Song et al.: a prompt-only novice can give 'expert-level explanations'. Unlearned agents behaved more like novices. Neither abstract gives numbers.
findings.relevance: A junior played by a frontier model will tend to fill gaps silently with its own stack knowledge instead of asking, which defeats the mechanism. The artifact-only context helps, but the persona needs explicit checks for assumptions.

findings.claim: Learning by teaching can improve a teacher LLM, including strong teachers teaching weaker students. The improvement signal is the students' measured performance on exam problems, not the students' report that they understood.
findings.source: Ning et al. 2024, 'Can LLMs Learn by Teaching for Better Reasoning? A Preliminary Study', NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv 2406.14629)
findings.evidence: M1 on 181 MATH problems, self-consistency -> LbT scoring: GPT-4o teaching GPT-4o mini 91.71->96.69; GPT-4o teaching LLaMA3-8B 91.71->95.03; LLaMA3-70B teaching LLaMA3-8B 81.77->87.85. 'Strong teachers can improve even when teaching weaker students.' Teaching material that students learn from more easily has 'clearer, more accurate logic'. M3 gains were modest (about 61->67 F1), and the authors call these 'preliminary case studies'.
findings.relevance: This supports making the junior a cheaper model, and the claim that explanations a novice can follow are better explanations. It also suggests a better stopping signal: test the junior with scenario questions graded against ground truth, rather than accepting 'I understand'.

findings.claim: Multi-agent debate gains are real in some setups, but most of them come from extra samples or majority voting. Debates often converge on wrong answers, and a single agent with strong prompts largely matches them.
findings.source: Du et al. 2023 (arXiv 2305.14325); Liang et al. 2023 (arXiv 2305.19118); Smit et al. 2023 (arXiv 2311.17371); Wang et al. 2024 (arXiv 2402.18272); Choi, Zhu & Li 2025, 'Debate or Vote', NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight (arXiv 2508.17536)
findings.evidence: Du (gpt-3.5, 3 agents, 2 rounds): GSM8K single agent 77.0, reflection 75.0, majority 81.0, debate 85.0. Debate answers 'were not necessarily correct', and agents confidently affirmed wrong consensus answers. Huang Table 7 at matched responses: self-consistency with 9 samples 88.2 vs debate 83.0. Choi: 'Majority Voting alone accounts for most of the performance gains typically attributed to MAD', and debate 'induces a martingale over agents' belief trajectories'. Wang: a 'single-agent LLM with strong prompts' achieves 'almost the same performance'. Smit: MAD does 'not reliably outperform' other prompting and is 'more sensitive to different hyperparameter settings'. Liang: self-reflection suffers 'Degeneration-of-Thought' and needs an adaptive break.
findings.relevance: Multi-agent formats must be compared against baselines with the same compute, such as single-agent explain-to-a-novice self-review or several independent plans. Otherwise any gain may just come from more tokens.

findings.claim: The bottleneck in self-correction is locating the error, not fixing it. Given the error's location, models correct well, and they correct errors attributed to an external source far more often than the same errors attributed to themselves.
findings.source: Tyen et al. 2024, 'LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location', ACL 2024 Findings (arXiv 2311.08516); Tsui 2025, 'Self-Correction Bench', listed as accepted to COLM 2026 (arXiv 2507.02778)
findings.evidence: Tyen, BIG-Bench Mistake overall mistake-finding accuracy: GPT-4 52.87% (step-level), GPT-3.5-Turbo 14.78%, PaLM 2 Unicorn 23.67%. Backtracking with oracle locations on originally incorrect traces: +18 to +44 points, e.g. tracking shuffled objects +43.92 (random locations +20.39). Tsui: models 'correct external errors but fail on identical internal ones', a '64.5% Self-Correction Blind Spot' across 14 open non-reasoning models. Appending 'Wait' cut it by 89.3%.
findings.relevance: This is the most plausible way Junior-dev could beat plain self-review. Questions tied to a specific diagram node or step localize gaps, and coming from another agent they may trigger correction that self-review does not. Both effects are untested for plans.

design_implications: Do not use the junior's 'I understand' as the stopping rule or the success metric. LLM verifiers approve flawed plans (84% false positives), and a single expert answering a non-expert barely beats no expert at all (f3, f10, f1). Stop at a hard round cap of 2-3 rounds, which matches Liang's adaptive break and Qi's finding that greater depth did not help (f15, f6). Better still, close with a teach-back test: the junior predicts system behavior for concrete scenarios, and a grader with repo access scores the predictions (f14).

Ground every answer. The main agent must answer each question from repo evidence (file paths, symbols, commands run) or mark it as an UNKNOWN/ASSUMPTION that becomes an open item in the plan, never a fluent invented answer. External, tool-grounded feedback is the ingredient the literature shows matters (f1, f4, f5). Explanations can rationalize (f12), and a persuasive consultant misleads a non-expert (f10).

Answer questions apart from the draft. Answer each question by checking the repo directly, not by re-reading the plan text, then reconcile the result with the plan. CoVe found that answering verification questions with the draft in view tends to repeat its errors (f6).

Require a classification for every question. The main agent records whether the plan already covered it (cite where), it exposed a gap (add the missing piece), it exposed an error (fix it, with evidence), or it is out of scope. This guards against sycophantic plan changes; models flip 32-86% of answers when challenged (f11). Keep the junior's questions neutral in tone, consistent with the non-adversarial intent.

Make questions localize. Each question must cite a specific node, edge or step in the plan or diagram and say what the junior expected to happen there. Error location is what unlocks correction (f16), and narrow questions are answered far more accurately than long-form ones (f6).

Control persona leakage. Have the junior narrate step by step how one request or data item flows through the diagram, and list every assumption it had to make, so that silent gap-filling becomes visible questions (f13). Consider a fresh junior context per round to limit multi-turn leakage (f13), and have it restate the system in its own words.

Plan for question quality to be the bottleneck. Models find the right missing piece only 40-50% of the time on planning tasks, and almost never ask unless told to (f7, f8). Prompt the junior explicitly to ask, perhaps with light coverage prompts (data flow, state ownership, ordering, failure paths, interfaces) worded as curiosity rather than critique, and measure how many seeded gaps its questions touch.

Evaluate with ground truth, not impressions. Build plans and diagrams with seeded defects of known types (missing step, wrong ordering, wrong component responsibility, missing failure path, invented API), plus clean control plans. Measure: (a) whether a question touches the defect, (b) whether the revised plan repairs it, (c) false or unnecessary changes to clean plans, (d) new invented facts checked against the repo, and (e) downstream implementation outcomes. Grade blind. A plan that merely reads more completely is not the target (f2, f3).

Test the weaker-model claim directly; do not assume it. Evidence leans toward weaker models benefiting less (f1 Llama-2, f2 Vicuna, f4 Code Llama, f5 StarCoder), and Haiku extracted as much information as Sonnet but made worse use of it (f8). Run a 2x2: main agent (Haiku, Sonnet) by junior (Haiku, Sonnet), and record integration failures, meaning answers the revised plan does not reflect. A cheaper junior is plausible (f14, f10) but question quality matters (f4, f7).

Include matched-compute baselines. Compare against a single-agent prompt to explain the plan step by step to a novice and fix gaps, against independent replanning or several plans, and against a generic reviewer subagent. Debate gains often reduce to extra samples (f15, f1). A separate detector agent did beat a single agent with an ask tool on SWE-bench (f8), which justifies testing the subagent design rather than assuming it.

Budget and record cost. Socratic sub-questioning used 9-19 calls per instance (f6), and the multi-agent clarification setup cost about 1.7x per task (f8). Report tokens and dollars per verified plan defect repaired, and per false change introduced.
open_questions: No study tests a questioner that sees only an architectural plan or diagram, nor measures plan-correctness gains from explaining to a novice. All the evidence here is analogical: math or QA self-correction, Blocksworld plans, clarification of SWE-bench issues, persona simulation.
Does a questioner who sees only the artifact find more real gaps than a reviewer with full context, or than the author's own explain-to-a-novice self-review, at matched cost?

In most clarification studies the answerer holds the ground truth (a simulated user with the full spec). In Junior-dev the answerer is the author of a possibly flawed plan. How much of the clarification benefit (f8, f9) survives when the answerer can be wrong?
Does the non-adversarial, curious framing reduce sycophantic plan changes and defensive confabulation compared with a critic framing, or does it just produce fewer questions about real flaws?
For Haiku as main agent, which fails more often: answering accurately, or folding correct answers back into the plan? Can a structured revision step close the integration gap seen in Ambig-SWE?

What is the right stopping signal? Candidates are a teach-back or scenario exam graded against the repo, a fixed round cap, or the point where new questions stop changing the plan. How do these compare against seeded-defect detection?

How much does persona leakage, the junior silently filling gaps with its own stack knowledge, suppress questions in practice? Would a deliberately weaker or smaller junior model ask more useful novice questions than a frontier model role-playing a novice?

Several sources here are preprints or have venues I could only see on arXiv or NeurIPS listing pages (Valmeekam, Khan, Kenton, Sharma, Du, Wang, Smit, the 2026 persona-leakage papers). Effect sizes come from single studies and were not reproduced.

r.summary:
The premise is well supported: LLM-written architecture plans and diagrams are incomplete in ways a reader could catch. Two diagram studies agree on the main defects: components are left out or lumped together, components that were never asked for get added, components land in the wrong layer, and relationships (edges) are missing or point the wrong way. Edge F1 was only 0.09 to 0.18 across frontier models. Software designs also quietly assume defaults, and agents rarely ask about missing facts unless told to.

The evidence for role-based questioning as the fix is thin and indirect:
- ChatDev's "communicative dehallucination" is the only ablation that isolates a questioning step. It raised a composite quality score from 0.309 to 0.395, but with GPT-3.5, proxy metrics and no variance reported. In that design the questioner is the agent who will do the work, not a separate novice.
- MetaGPT deliberately replaced chat between roles with structured documents.
- MAST lists "fail to ask for clarification" as a real failure mode (6.8% of failures). It also finds that the checks agents make on each other are often superficial and that prompt or topology fixes help only modestly.
- In the clarification studies (Ambig-SWE, HumanEvalComm), asking helps because the answerer holds information the agent lacks. Junior-dev breaks that condition: the answers come from the same model that wrote the plan, so there is no new ground truth.

Three weak links stand out:
1. **The junior may not notice gaps.** LLMs rarely detect underspecification without prompting, and an LLM playing a novice tends to behave like an "idealized novice" that fills gaps from expert knowledge.
2. **The main agent's answers may be wrong.** LLM verifiers of plans give many false positives: 38 of 45 invalid Blocksworld plans were judged valid. LLMs are poor at finding their own errors, though they fix them well once shown where they are.
3. **Revisions may break correct parts.** Weaker models get swayed by other agents' wrong feedback and flip answers when challenged (46% of the time, with a 17% accuracy drop). Backtracking on reasoning that was already correct lost up to 11 points.

The most plausible working mechanism is narrower than the user's hypothesis. Questions asked by an agent that sees only the artifact work like independent verification questions (factored Chain-of-Verification roughly doubled precision) and like pointers to where the plan breaks down. They help only if the answers are grounded in the real code and written back into the artifact.

The repository's R6 report (planner-executor-split.md) implies two things:
- Plans by weaker models have the most gaps, and plan quality scales with the planner. A subpar plan can be worse than none, and package-level architecture without implementation detail transfers poorly. So Haiku and Sonnet plans have the most to gain, but those authors are also the least reliable at answering and revising.
- Every hybrid that preserved quality kept a strong model, or verification, in the loop.

Practitioner prior art is close (Matt Pocock's grilling skill, superpowers' "write for an engineer who has not seen this codebase", requests for a fresh-context plan reviewer) but all of it is anecdotal. No study tests explaining an architecture plan to a simulated novice.

findings.claim: ChatDev's communicative dehallucination is the only multi-agent ablation found that isolates a questioning step. Before answering, the assistant asks the instructor for specifics. Removing the step lowered every metric, but the gain is modest and the setup is weak.
findings.source: Qian et al., ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development, ACL 2024 (arXiv 2307.07924v5)
findings.evidence: Defined as encouraging 'the assistant to actively seek more detailed suggestions from the instructor before delivering a formal response' via 'role reversal'. Table 4: full ChatDev Completeness 0.5600 / Executability 0.8800 / Consistency 0.8021 / Quality 0.3953 vs without CDH 0.4700 / 0.8400 / 0.7983 / 0.3094. Model: 'ChatGPT-3.5 with a temperature of 0.2'. Completeness = share of software with no 'placeholder' code; Consistency is embedding similarity; Quality is the product of the three. No variance reported. The authors say removing all roles had the largest impact and that agent capability 'might be overestimated'. In code review, 'Method Not Implemented' was 34.85% of reviewer–programmer discussions.
findings.relevance: This is the closest measured analogue to Junior-dev, but the questioner is the executing agent asking for details it needs, not a separate novice asking the author to explain. The ~22% relative quality gain (my arithmetic) comes with GPT-3.5, proxy metrics that reward the absence of placeholders, and one run. It does not show that architectural logic improves.

findings.claim: Across 1,642 multi-agent traces, failing to ask for clarification is a recurring failure mode. Agents also check each other only superficially, and better roles or topology help only modestly.
findings.source: Cemri et al., Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST), arXiv 2503.13657v3
findings.evidence: 7 frameworks; taxonomy kappa = 0.88. FM-2.2 'Fail to ask for clarification' 6.80%; FM-2.6 Reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%; FM-3.2 No or incomplete verification 8.20%; FM-3.3 Incorrect verification 9.10%; FM-3.1 Premature termination 6.20%; FM-1.5 Unaware of termination conditions 12.4%; FM-1.3 Step repetition 15.7%. 'many existing verifiers perform only superficial checks, despite being prompted to perform thorough verification'. Overall failure rates 41% to 86.7%. Table 5, ChatDev ProgramDev-v0: baseline 25.0, improved prompt 34.4, new topology 40.6. The authors say these 'do not constitute substantial improvements'.
findings.relevance: This supports the idea that missing clarification hurts. It also warns that role-based agents verify superficially and handle termination badly: premature stops, unknown stop conditions and repetition. Junior-dev's 'until the junior understands' stopping rule is exactly that risk.

findings.claim: MetaGPT reduced errors by replacing free-form chat between roles with structured documents (PRD, system design) and adding executable feedback. Its role ablation favours more roles, but on small, coarse measures.
findings.source: Hong et al., MetaGPT: Meta Programming for a Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework, ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2308.00352v6)
findings.evidence: Table 3 (Engineer only → all four roles): Revisions 10 → 2.5, Executability 1.0 → 4.0, Expense $0.915 → $1.385; Executability is not monotonic (PM+Architect 2.5, PM+Project Manager 2.0). The paper says 'agents in MetaGPT communicate through documents and diagrams (structured outputs) rather than dialogue' and that SOPs reduce 'the risk of hallucinations caused by idle chatter between LLMs'. Without executable feedback, Human Revision Cost was 2.25 vs 0.83 with it. The ablation's sample size was not visible in the extracted text. No ablation compares documents with chat directly.
findings.relevance: MetaGPT's designers treated unstructured Q&A between roles as a source of hallucination and fixed it with structured artifacts plus execution. For Junior-dev this suggests the value lies in what gets written back into the plan, not in the conversation itself.

findings.claim: LLM-generated architecture and UML diagrams systematically omit and over-abstract components, invent components nobody asked for, misplace boundaries, and get relationships wrong. Conflicts can hide behind vague nodes.
findings.source: Li et al., Benchmarking Requirement-to-Architecture Generation with Hybrid Evaluation (R2ABench), arXiv 2604.06683 (read v1; current v3, Sept 2026); Ferrari, Abualhaija, Arora, Model Generation with LLMs: From Requirements to UML Sequence Diagrams, arXiv 2404.06371v2 (2024)
findings.evidence: R2ABench, 17 PRDs, full-PRD direct generation: Node F1 0.54–0.67 and Edge F1 0.0855–0.1760 across GPT-5, Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Gemini-2.5-Pro, DeepSeek-V3.2 and Qwen3-coder; orphan ratio 12.64–20.25%. Failure modes: E1 node omission (Claude-Sonnet-4.6 reduced a 20+ node Business Logic Layer to five coarse nodes), E2 hallucination injection (e.g., a log aggregator added by GPT-5), E3 boundary misplacement, E4 relational failure: missing edges, reversed data flow, 'structurally fragmented architectures'. Removing the architecture section raised orphan ratio from 15.96% to 20.23%. Agent frameworks gave volatile results. Ferrari et al., ChatGPT (GPT-3.5), 87 sequence diagrams, kappa 0.67: Completeness 3.63/5, Correctness 3.22/5 (not significantly above 3), understandability 4.37. Examples include missing conditions ('If 10 player statistics are already recorded' ignored), invented terms ('Study Results' 'never mentioned'), and 'Inconsistent requirements were concealed' behind a function call 'Determine selected value'.
findings.relevance: This is direct evidence for the user's premise and a ready defect taxonomy for questions and evals. Diagrams read well and parse, but their relational and conditional logic is weak, which is exactly what tracing questions ('what calls this, with what data, and what happens if it fails?') would probe. Both samples are small: 17 PRDs and 87 diagrams.

findings.claim: On underspecified SWE-bench tasks, interacting with a simulated user who holds the missing facts recovers much of the lost performance. Models almost never ask without being prompted, telling whether a task is underspecified is unreliable below Sonnet-class, and question quality depends on the model.
findings.source: Vijayvargiya et al., Ambig-SWE: Interactive Agents to Overcome Underspecificity in Software Engineering, arXiv 2502.13069v3
findings.evidence: 500 SWE-bench Verified issues, each fully specified and underspecified. The GPT-4o user proxy holds the full issue and 'responds only using information explicitly present in it'. Interaction boosts underspecified performance 'up to 74% over the non-interactive settings'; Claude Sonnet 4 recovers 89% of full-spec performance. 'Without explicit prompting, models almost never interact, even for severely underspecified inputs.' Detection accuracy: Sonnet 4 0.89, Sonnet 3.5 0.84, Haiku 3.5 0.63, Llama 3.1 70B 0.52, Qwen 3 Coder 0.50. Haiku 3.5 'follows a rigid three-question template regardless of context'; Llama asked 'too few questions' with 'overly general phrasing'. Effective questions are 'specific, actionable, and task-level'. The authors conclude that prompt engineering alone is insufficient.
findings.relevance: Questioning pays off when the answerer holds ground truth. In Junior-dev the answerer is the plan's author, so answers add knowledge only if the author consults the repo or the user. The results also argue for a Sonnet-class junior even when the main agent is Haiku.

findings.claim: Code LLMs mostly produce code instead of asking clarifying questions when problem descriptions are ambiguous, inconsistent or incomplete. An explicit question-asking agent raises the ask rate but also asks unnecessary questions.
findings.source: Wu and Fard, Benchmarking the Communication Competence of Code Generation for LLMs and LLM Agent (HumanEvalComm), ACM TOSEM (arXiv 2406.00215v3)
findings.evidence: 'more than 60% of responses from Code LLMs still generate code rather than ask questions'. Communication Rate: ChatGPT 14.21%, DeepSeek Coder 30.76%, Okanagan (ChatGPT base) 72.73%. Good Question Rate: ChatGPT 13.43% → Okanagan 52.24%. Pass@1 drops 35–52% on modified problems. 'Okanagan sometimes still asks questions that appear to be unnecessary' on complete problems. '95% of responses... still generate code even when 50% of problem descriptions are randomly removed.'
findings.relevance: Models do not naturally flag what they don't understand; a dedicated asking role is needed, which supports a separate junior. The same role over-asks, so the junior needs a way to separate real gaps from noise. Without one, it can generate many low-value rounds.

findings.claim: Verification questions answered without seeing the original draft reduce hallucination more than questions answered with the draft in view. This supports the principle of a questioner that sees only the artifact.
findings.source: Dhuliawala et al., Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in Large Language Models, arXiv 2309.11495v2 (Findings of ACL 2024)
findings.evidence: Llama 65B. Wikidata list precision: few-shot baseline 0.17, CoVe joint 0.29, 2-step 0.36, factored 0.32. MultiSpanQA F1: 0.39 → joint 0.46, factored 0.48. FactScore: 55.9 → joint 60.8, factored 63.7, factor+revise 71.4. Rationale: 'verifying questions should not attend to the original baseline response as they may be prone to repeating it'.
findings.relevance: This is the best-measured mechanism for Junior-dev's isolation choice. A reader without the author's context is less likely to repeat the author's mistakes. But in CoVe the same model answers the questions independently. In Junior-dev the author answers with full context, which reintroduces the bias CoVe removes unless the answers are grounded.

findings.claim: Making a model explain its own code line by line ('rubber duck' self-debugging) helps, but explanation without execution feedback gives small, inconsistent gains. Most of the improvement comes from running the code.
findings.source: Chen, Lin, Schärli, Zhou, Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug, ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2304.05128)
findings.evidence: Spider (no unit tests), Simple → +Expl: Codex 81.3 → 84.1, GPT-3.5 72.2 → 72.2, GPT-4 73.4 → 73.6. Table 3, without unit-test execution: TransCoder Codex Simple 83.4 → +Expl 83.9, GPT-3.5 89.1 → 89.1, GPT-4 78.2 → 78.0; MBPP Codex 57.6 → 64.4, GPT-3.5 68.2 → 68.2, GPT-4 76.0 → 76.0. The paper's own words: code explanation 'consistently improves the baseline by 2 - 3%' on Spider, and 'models generally benefit from richer feedback... especially when the execution information is present'. I extracted the PDF text locally.
findings.relevance: Explaining to someone else, the core of Junior-dev, gives an LLM only a small self-check benefit unless it is tied to real feedback. The user's hypothesis needs an extra source of truth, such as the repo, tests or the user, to deliver large gains.

findings.claim: LLMs are poor at finding errors in their own plans and reasoning. An LLM plan verifier waves through most invalid plans, yet the same models fix errors well once shown where they are. Revising steps that were already correct costs accuracy.
findings.source: Valmeekam, Marquez, Kambhampati, Can Large Language Models Really Improve by Self-critiquing Their Own Plans? (arXiv 2310.08118, 2023); Tyen et al., LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (arXiv 2311.08516v3, Findings of ACL 2024)
findings.evidence: Valmeekam (GPT-4, 100 Blocksworld instances, PDF text extracted locally): LLM+LLM with backprompting 55/100; LLM+VAL (sound verifier) 88/100; generator only 40/100. The verifier LLM judged 38 of 45 invalid plans valid ('38/45 (84.45%)' false positive rate). Tyen: overall mistake-finding accuracy GPT-4 39.80/52.87/43.40%, GPT-3.5-Turbo 10.44/14.78/14.31%. Backtracking with the oracle mistake location (PaLM 2) gave +18.04 to +43.92 on traces with wrong answers, but −0.00 to −11.43 on traces with correct answers; a random location gave smaller gains.
findings.relevance: If the main agent judges whether its own plan must change, expect it to say 'fine' too often. Junior-dev's best case is pinpointing where understanding breaks, which is the location signal that makes correction work. Every revision also risks damaging correct parts.

findings.claim: Weaker models are easily swayed by other agents' incorrect feedback, and LLMs in general change correct answers when challenged.
findings.source: Chen et al., AgentVerse (ICLR 2024, arXiv 2308.10848); Laban et al., Are You Sure? Challenging LLMs Leads to Performance Drops in The FlipFlop Experiment (arXiv 2311.08596)
findings.evidence: AgentVerse: for GPT-3.5-Turbo 'the Group setup underperforms the Solo setup in two of three tasks', attributed to 'susceptibility to erroneous feedback': 'Agent A, despite starting with a correct answer, would be easily swayed by Agent B's incorrect feedback'; about '10% of errors in the MGSM dataset' trace to this, and the pattern is absent for GPT-4. On HumanEval, group discussion still helped (GPT-3.5 74.4 → 75.6; GPT-4 87.2 → 89.0, confounded by an added unit-test agent). FlipFlop (abstract only): 'models flip their answers on average 46% of the time', average accuracy drop 17%, ten LLMs on seven classification tasks.
findings.relevance: Junior-dev's question batches are not adversarial, but a confused junior's question can read as an implied objection. A Haiku or Sonnet main agent may 'accommodate' a misunderstanding by changing a correct design. The 'decide whether to change' step needs safeguards.

findings.claim: Prompting an LLM to act as a novice does not remove its expertise. It behaves like an 'idealized novice', and general prompting tends to yield correct, near-perfect output.
findings.source: Simulating Students' Java Programming Errors with Large Language Models, EDM 2026 short paper (arXiv 2606.14113); Song, Guo, Lin, Simulating Novice Students Using Machine Unlearning and Relearning in LLMs (arXiv 2603.26142)
findings.evidence: EDM paper: general prompting 'typically yields correct or near-perfect solutions, entirely missing the characteristic flaws inherent to novice code'; 'the LLM behaves like an idealized novice'. Error distribution skews: Condition Logic 46.4% LLM vs 24.9% human; 'Other' 7.1% vs 28.3%. Five models including claude-sonnet-4 and gpt-5. Unlearning paper: 'even when prompted to "act like a novice," the LLMs can still produce expert-level explanations'; 'prompt-based role assignment does not alter the model's underlying pre-trained knowledge'. Its prompt-only vs unlearning comparison numbers were not in the text I read.
findings.relevance: A 'junior with no experience in this stack' will silently fill gaps with standard defaults, such as assuming a queue retries or a cache invalidates, instead of asking. Junior-dev should rest on an explicit rule ('anything not stated in the artifact is unknown; ask about it') rather than on persona realism.

findings.claim: Simulated interviews can surface needs and ask questions that build on earlier answers. The evidence is small-scale, and the LLM interviewer still makes mistakes and invents things.
findings.source: Ataei et al., Elicitron: An LLM Agent-Based Simulation Framework for Design Requirements Elicitation (arXiv 2404.16045, 2024); Korn, Gorsch, Vogelsang, LLMREI: Automating Requirements Elicitation Interviews with LLMs (RE 2025, arXiv 2507.02564)
findings.evidence: Elicitron (a tent product; 20 agents per condition; ~$2.4): latent needs per condition M = 8.825 / 9.875 / 10.875; 'identifying a greater number of latent needs than conventional human interviews' (abstract), but the human baseline lacked variance, so 'we could not conduct any statistical test'. LLMREI (GPT-4o, 33 interviews, ground truth of 12 and 8 requirements): fully elicited 'up to 60.94 %' (+12.76% partially); context-deepening plus context-enhancing questions 59.7% (short prompt) vs 42.7% (long) (my arithmetic); the bot hallucinated 'an estimated project price'.
findings.relevance: There is precedent that LLM-run interviews done in rounds elicit information beyond the first statement. Recall stayed well below 100% and the interviewer still made mistakes. The prompt design changed how far questions built on earlier answers, a variable worth testing for the junior.
