findings.claim: The closest practitioner prior art (Matt Pocock's grilling skill, superpowers' writing-plans skill, plan-review workflows, requests for a fresh-context plan reviewer in Claude Code) closely matches Junior-dev's mechanics but reports no measurements.
findings.source: mattpocock/skills 'grilling' and 'grill-me' SKILL.md v1.3.2 (local plugin cache); superpowers 'writing-plans' SKILL.md v7.0.2 (local); G. Jiang, 'Reviewing Claude Code's work: review the plan, the execution, or both' (blog, updated 2026-04-20); claudeissues.com mirror of a 2026-07-02 Claude Code feature request
findings.evidence: Grilling (read locally at C:/Users/godle/.claude/plugins/cache/mattpocock/mattpocock-skills/1.3.2/skills/productivity/grilling/SKILL.md): 'Work the tree in rounds. The frontier is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled... Ask the whole frontier in one round'; 'The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed.' It interviews the user, who owns the decisions; facts are found by sub-agents. Writing-plans: 'Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec... What they cannot know is what you decided.' Blog: 'the reviewer should not be the builder'; it reports no plan problems caught and 'Measurement: None'. Feature request for 'fresh-context adversarial plan-review in plan mode': seen only as a search snippet (the mirror failed DNS), so unverified.
findings.relevance: The round, frontier and termination design is already worked out in grilling and can be adapted. Two differences from Junior-dev matter: grilling's answerer is the human decision owner, and practitioner reviewers are critics, not novices. No one has published outcome data, so Junior-dev must produce its own.

findings.claim: This repository's R6 review finds that plan quality scales with the planner and that a subpar plan can be worse than none. High-level design does not transfer without implementation detail, implementation holds real decisions a plan written beforehand misses, and the hybrids that keep quality keep a strong model or verifier in the loop.
findings.source: docs/research/planner-executor-split.md (R6, issue #36, 2026-11-07), this repository
findings.evidence: DCAS (ASE '26): Qwen3-Coder-30B no plan 42.8, self-plan 48.2, Sonnet 4.5 plan 57.8; the authors say plan quality 'scales with planner capability'. Liu et al. (2604.12147): 'a subpar plan hurts performance even more than no plan at all', and capable models override plans that do not fit. RealBench: removing class diagrams dropped Claude Sonnet 4 from 17.5% to 6.2%; high-level design 'is insufficient without implementation details'. 'Every hybrid that preserved quality kept the strong model active during or after execution.' R2 §2.4 (as cited): weak readers are the most misled by wrong context. The repo README notes the 2026-11-08 pilot found Haiku within noise of Sonnet with a full test suite.
findings.relevance: Haiku and Sonnet plans have the most gaps to expose, which fits the user's hypothesis. But the same weaker author answers and revises, and a confidently fleshed-out wrong plan is the 'subpar plan' that hurts. The junior also cannot see code, so it cannot surface the point-of-edit decisions (reuse, layer, invariants) that R6 found plans miss. A strong model in the loop is the best-supported lever.

findings.claim: Persona framing alone does not reliably improve LLM performance; its effects are largely random. Gains credited to multi-agent conversation often come from extra samples or voting rather than the dialogue.
findings.source: Zheng et al., When 'A Helpful Assistant' Is Not Really Helpful: Personas in System Prompts Do Not Improve Performances of LLMs (arXiv 2311.10054); Choi, Zhu, Li, Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent LLMs? (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2508.17536v2)
findings.evidence: Zheng et al. (abstract): 162 roles, 4 LLM families, 2,410 factual questions; 'adding personas in system prompts does not improve model performance'; 'the effect of each persona can be largely random'; automatically identifying the best persona 'is challenging'. Choi et al. (abstract): 'Majority Voting alone accounts for most of the performance gains typically attributed to MAD' across 'seven NLP benchmarks'; debate 'induces a martingale over agents' belief trajectories', so it does not raise expected correctness on its own.
findings.relevance: The 'junior developer' label and the non-adversarial framing should not be assumed to matter; test them as ablations. Any Junior-dev gain must beat token-matched controls, such as self-review or extra sampling, before it can be credited to novice Q&A.

design_implications: Make the junior's method explicit rather than relying on the persona. Have it trace every component, edge and step in the artifact and ask what triggers it, what data comes in and goes out, who owns it, and what happens on failure. Tell it that anything not stated in the artifact is unknown and must not be filled with standard defaults, and require each question to cite the plan line, node or edge it is about. Role-played novices leak expertise, and persona labels have random effects. (f11, f15, f4)

Aim the questions at the known weak spots of LLM diagrams: missing or reversed edges and data flow, components lumped into coarse nodes, components nobody asked for, wrong-layer boundaries, dropped conditions or branches, and vague nodes that hide conflicts (e.g., 'Determine selected value'). Diagrams usually parse and look tidy, so questions about readability or syntax add little. (f4)

Keep the junior isolated from the repo and the conversation, as planned; this matches factored verification. But require every answer that adds information to be written back into the artifact, or explicitly marked out of scope. The finishing test should be a fresh junior that reads only the revised artifact with no Q&A history, not the original junior's statement that it understands, because that understanding may live only in the chat. (f7, f3, f2)

Ground the main agent's answers. Let it consult the repo, tests or user when it answers. Answers the author produces from the same context add no new ground truth, and LLM self-verification gives many false positives. Questioning helped in Ambig-SWE because the answerer held real information. (f5, f8, f9)

Split 'answer' from 'revise'. For each question, the main agent labels it: already answered by the plan (point to where), gap the plan must state, error found, or out of scope. It changes the plan only for gaps and errors, with a one-line justification, and must not change parts the question merely touches. This guards against sycophantic flips and against damage from revising correct steps, which hits weaker main agents hardest. (f10, f9, f14)

Choose the junior model by question quality, not cost. Ambig-SWE found Haiku 3.5 used a rigid three-question template while Sonnet asked about behaviour. Default the junior to Sonnet-class even when the main agent is Haiku, and evaluate a Haiku junior as a separate arm. (f5, f6)

Borrow grilling's structure (rounds over a frontier of questions whose prerequisites are settled, numbered questions, done when nothing is left silently assumed) and add hard limits: a maximum number of rounds and of questions per batch, a filter for duplicate and low-value questions, and an explicit stop condition. MAST shows that role-based agents stop early, ignore stop conditions or repeat steps, and question-asking agents over-ask. (f13, f2, f6)

Evaluate on artifacts with seeded defects and known ground truth, using the R2ABench defect types plus omitted failure paths and unstated assumptions. Measure three things: recall of the seeded defects that questions surface, precision of revisions (were correct parts changed, and did new errors appear), and the rounds and tokens spent. (f4, f9, f10)

Include controls that rule out simple explanations: no review; the same model explaining its own plan step by step in the same context (rubber duck); a generic fresh-context critic (adversarial review); and a token-matched arm that spends the same budget on extra plan samples or self-review. Junior-dev is supported only if it beats these, especially the critic and the token-matched arm. (f15, f8, f1)

Test the 'helps weaker models' claim directly. Use Haiku, Sonnet and a stronger model as plan authors and measure the share of the gap to a strong-model plan or revision that Junior-dev closes. Measure downstream implementation outcomes, not just plan completeness, because a confidently fleshed-out wrong plan can be worse than none. Score reuse, duplication and wrong-layer edits, which tests miss. (f14, f1)

State Junior-dev's purpose without performance claims until the evaluation exists. The questioning-step evidence is a single GPT-3.5 ablation on proxy metrics plus practitioner anecdotes, so present it as a hypothesis in the skill's documentation. (f1, f13, f15)
open_questions: Does the junior actually detect gaps in a plan, or does it fill them with standard defaults? No study measures how well an LLM role-playing a novice detects gaps in software plans or diagrams.
Without new grounding, how often are the main agent's answers correct versus fluent confabulations? Does consulting the repo while answering change that rate?
Does a confused question cause Haiku or Sonnet main agents to change correct design decisions, and does the non-adversarial framing reduce that compared with a critic?
Is 'the junior says it understands' a valid stopping signal, or do LLM juniors declare understanding too early? Would a fresh-context re-read of the revised artifact be a better stopping criterion?
Does a better plan after Q&A lead to better implementations? The repo's R6 evidence says many decisive choices are made at the point of edit, which a junior that sees only the plan cannot see.
Is the benefit actually larger for weaker authors? Weaker authors leave more gaps but are also worse at answering and revising, so the net effect could go either way.
Which junior model gives the best value for the cost (Haiku vs Sonnet), and how many rounds and tokens until convergence?
Do junior questions surface defects a critic misses (e.g., implicit data flow, missing failure paths), or do the two find the same defects? No head-to-head comparison exists.
The Ambig-SWE and HumanEvalComm results use older models (Claude 3.5 or 4-era, GPT-3.5). Do current Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 still behave the same way when asking and detecting gaps?

r.summary:
Evaluation methodology for Junior-dev (2026-11-12). I read the repository's conventions (evaluation-protocol.md, the hygiene eval README, the activation-eval README, capability-gradient.md, and the 2026-11-08 pilot report) and about 20 primary sources this session. Five conclusions follow.

(1) A holistic LLM judge would be biased toward Junior-dev by design. The revised plan is longer, and the main agent and the judge are often the same family. Length bias, position bias and self-preference are replicated. Self-preference also survives in rubric-style binary grading: judges were more than 50% more likely to wrongly pass their own failed rubric items. Grading should therefore be per item against a hidden ledger of required details, mechanical where possible, with a cross-family or ensemble judge, blinded to arm and calibrated against human labels.

(2) The no-review baseline is the wrong main comparison. Studies of self-correction and multi-agent discussion show that matched-compute single-agent alternatives often match multi-agent schemes: a strong prompt, a same-budget self-revision, or simply putting the feedback into the first instruction. Self-revision can also degrade answers. The decisive contrast is Junior-dev against a token-matched "reread and revise as if explaining to a newcomer" arm, and against a one-pass "write it so a junior could follow" instruction. The second arm tests whether the effect is just the instruction.

(3) There are good templates for seeded-gap cases with known answers: HumanEvalComm (incomplete, inconsistent and ambiguous rewrites), Ambig-SWE (Full, Hidden and Interaction settings with an informed simulated user), TravelPlanner (scripted per-constraint checks with micro and strict pass rates), and seeded-omission requirements studies. The mechanism should be split into two parts: whether a question hits the gap, and whether the agent fixes it once pointed there. LLMs are poor at finding errors but much better at fixing them once told where they are, so these two parts can fail independently.

(4) Downstream implementation by a pinned executor, graded by hidden tests, does discriminate plan quality (DCAS; Gandhi et al.). It needs an executor in its headroom band, and it is costly, so it belongs in confirmation, not in every hill-climb iteration.

(5) Variance is large relative to plausible effects. Single runs differ by 2-6 pp, clustered standard errors can be 3 times the naive ones, a different simulated-user model shifts outcomes by up to 9 pp, and prompt optimisation overfits dev sets by 5-20 pp. With 12-20 cases, only effects of about 15-20 pp are detectable.

The repository's own pilot is a warning. Its Sonnet-review-then-Haiku-revise arm cost $0.281 per passing step, against $0.077 for Haiku alone, and did no better. Only 1 of 6 steps separated the arms, and the skill rarely triggers on its own. No source tests a novice explainee as a plan-improvement intervention. The learning-by-teaching result is preliminary and on reasoning tasks, so the user's hypothesis remains untested.

findings.claim: LLM judges show position bias, verbosity bias and self-enhancement bias. Current judges are better but not free of them. Swapping the order and counting a win only when both orders agree is the standard mitigation.
findings.source: Zheng et al., 2023, 'Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena', NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks; Ye et al., 2025, 'Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge' (CALM), ICLR 2025
findings.evidence: Zheng (Table 2): position consistency with the default prompt was Claude-v1 23.8%, GPT-3.5 46.2%, GPT-4 65.0%. The paper says "Most LLM judges favor the first position." In the repetitive-list verbosity attack (Table 3, 23 answers), the failure rate was 91.3% for Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5 and 8.7% for GPT-4. The paper reports "GPT-4 favors itself with a 10% higher win rate; Claude-v1 favors itself with a 25% higher win rate", but says it "cannot determine whether the models exhibit a self-enhancement bias." Mitigations: "only declare a win when an answer is preferred in both orders"; few-shot prompting raised GPT-4 consistency from 65.0% to 77.5%. GPT-4 agreed with humans 85% (S2, no ties), against 81% human-to-human. CALM (arXiv 2410.02736v2, Table 7 default rows): position robustness rate was 0.776 for GPT-4o and 0.832 for Claude-3.5-Sonnet; verbosity robustness rate was 0.977 and 0.952. Self-enhancement error rate (Table 5) was 7.48% for Claude-3.5-Sonnet and 1.74% for GPT-4o. CALM: "most models rated their outputs more favorably, even when answer sources were anonymized."
findings.relevance: A holistic or pairwise comparison of a plan before and after Junior-dev is exposed to all three biases. The revised plan is longer, and the judge is often the same family as the main agent. A pairwise judgment is only usable with both orders and a consistency rule, and it should be secondary.

findings.claim: Length alone moves LLM-judge preferences by tens of points. Regression-based length control removes most of the swing.
findings.source: Dubois, Galambosi, Liang, Hashimoto, 2024, 'Length-Controlled AlpacaEval: A Simple Way to Debias Automatic Evaluators', COLM 2024
findings.evidence: "AlpacaEval is highly length gameable." For gpt4_1106_preview, prompting for concise, standard or verbose output gave win rates from 22.9% to 64.3% before length control, and 41.9% to 51.6% after. The normalized standard deviation across the prompts "decreases from 25% to 10%". The method fits a GLM and predicts "while conditioning the GLM with a zero difference in lengths". It raised Spearman correlation with Chatbot Arena from 0.94 to 0.98.
findings.relevance: Junior-dev's output is structurally longer, so any preference judgment will partly reward length. Plan length must be recorded and an estimate adjusted for length reported. A 'just add detail' arm is also needed, to show the rubric does not pay for padding.

findings.claim: Self-preference persists in rubric-based binary grading, the kind of checklist grading recommended here. It extends to the judge's model family, and ensembling judges reduces it without removing it.
findings.source: Pombal, Rei, Martins, 2026, 'Self-Preference Bias in Rubric-Based Evaluation of Large Language Models', arXiv 2604.06996; Wataoka et al., 2024, 'Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge', arXiv 2410.21819
findings.evidence: Pombal (abstract): on IFEval and LiveCodeBench rubrics that can be checked by program, among rubrics where generators fail, "judges can be more than 50% more likely to incorrectly mark them as satisfied when the output is their own." On HealthBench the bias skews scores "by up to 10 points". Judges "tend to favor outputs produced by themselves or by models from their own family". "ensembling multiple judges helps mitigate SPB, but without fully eliminating it." Wataoka: "GPT-4 exhibits a significant degree of self-preference bias"; "LLMs assign significantly higher evaluations to outputs with lower perplexity than human evaluators", whether or not the outputs were self-generated. I read only the abstracts of both papers.
findings.relevance: A checklist does not by itself protect against a Claude judge grading a Claude main agent's revised plan. Use mechanical checks where possible. Otherwise use a judge from another family or a cross-family ensemble, and audit judge errors against human labels per arm.

findings.claim: Structured checklist grading, with one isolated binary check per item and the strict all-items pass rate reported, raises agreement with humans. The gains are modest, and the checklists still need calibration against people.
findings.source: Cook et al., 2024, 'TICKing All the Boxes: Generated Checklists Improve LLM Evaluation and Generation', arXiv 2410.03608; Xie et al., 2024, 'TravelPlanner: A Benchmark for Real-World Planning with Language Agents', ICML 2024, arXiv 2402.01622; Anthropic, 'Demystifying evals for AI agents' (engineering guide)
findings.evidence: TICK: exact agreement between LLM judgments and human preferences rose "46.4% → 52.2%" with checklists, compared with direct scoring. Human inter-annotator agreement rose "0.194 → 0.256" when people used the checklists. TravelPlanner checks plans "automatically through pre-defined scripts". Its macro rate "calculates the ratio of plans that pass all commonsense or hard constraints among all tested plans", and Final Pass Rate counts plans that meet all constraints. "even GPT-4 only achieves a success rate of 0.6%." The Anthropic guide (vendor guidance) says "grade each dimension with an isolated LLM-as-judge rather than using one to grade all dimensions", "LLM-as-judge graders should be closely calibrated with human experts", and "it's often better to grade what the agent produced, not the path it took."
findings.relevance: This supports a hidden per-case ledger of required plan details, each graded alone, with item recall (micro) and strict all-gaps-closed (macro) reported separately. TICK's small agreement gain means the ledger and judge still need a human-labelled calibration sample.

findings.claim: Matched-compute single-agent alternatives often explain the gains credited to multi-agent schemes: self-revision, a stronger prompt, or putting the feedback into the first instruction. Self-revision without outside information can help (Self-Refine) or hurt (Huang).
findings.source: Huang et al., 2024, 'Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet', ICLR 2024; Wang et al., 2024, 'Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning: Are Multi-Agent Discussions the Key?', ACL 2024; Madaan et al., 2023, 'Self-Refine', NeurIPS 2023
findings.evidence: Huang: after intrinsic self-correction, GPT-3.5 fell on CommonSenseQA from 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1), and on GSM8K from 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7. With 9 responses, multi-agent debate scored 83.0 against 88.2 for self-consistency: "multi-agent debate significantly underperforms simple self-consistency using majority voting." The paper also says "simply integrating the feedback into the initial instruction can yield better results" and urges "an in-depth inference cost analysis." Wang (abstract): "a single-agent LLM with strong prompts can achieve almost the same performance as the best existing discussion approach". Discussion helps "only when there is no demonstration in the prompt." Self-Refine (abstract): "~20% absolute on average in task performance" across 7 tasks with GPT-3.5, ChatGPT and GPT-4. I read only the abstracts of Wang and Self-Refine.
findings.relevance: Junior-dev's main comparison must be a same-budget self-review and a one-pass instruction such as 'write this so a junior dev could follow it'. A no-review baseline is not enough. If the instruction arm matches Junior-dev, the subagent loop is not what produces the benefit.

findings.claim: LLMs find their own errors poorly, but correct much better once told where the error is. Corrections given a location also damage some answers that were already right.
findings.source: Tyen et al., 2024, 'LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location', Findings of ACL 2024, arXiv 2311.08516v3
findings.evidence: Table 4: the best mistake-finding accuracy was GPT-4 at 52.87 (direct, step-level); GPT-3.5-Turbo scored 14.78 and PaLM 2 Unicorn 23.67. Table 6: backtracking with the true mistake location (PaLM 2 Unicorn) improved traces that were originally wrong by +18.04 to +43.92 pp. Across the five tasks it changed traces that were originally right by 0 to −11.43 pp. The paper says "the gains from correcting incorrect traces are larger than losses from changing originally correct answers."
findings.relevance: This suggests a mechanism: a novice's questions could act as pointers to where the plan is weak, which is the step weak models do worst. The eval should log two things per gap: whether a question hit it, and whether the agent fixed it after the hit. It should also count damage to correct parts of the plan. An arm that tells the agent the gap locations directly gives a ceiling.

findings.claim: A seeded-gap clarification benchmark already exists for code. It rewrites problems to be incomplete, inconsistent or ambiguous, and measures question rate, question quality and final correctness with an LLM answerer that knows the original. Its LLM evaluator agrees well with humans but is lenient about question quality.
findings.source: Wu and Fard, 'HumanEvalComm: Benchmarking the Communication Competence of Code Generation for LLMs and LLM Agent', ACM TOSEM, arXiv 2406.00215v3
findings.evidence: The benchmark has 762 modified problems from HumanEval's 164: ambiguity 164, inconsistency 164, incompleteness 164, and combinations 162, 34 and 74. One engineer modified them and a second reviewed. Metrics are Communication Rate, Good Question Rate, Pass@1 and Test Pass Rate. A GPT-3.5 evaluator with both the original and modified problems answers the questions. In a human check, Cohen's kappa was 0.72–0.96, but the LLM evaluator "labeled more questions as 'Good' than human raters did". False Recovery Rate was 30–40% for most models. ChatGPT Pass@1 fell from 65.58% to 31.34% on the modified problems. Over 60% of responses still produced code instead of asking.
findings.relevance: This gives a ready taxonomy and metric set for seeded plan gaps (incomplete, inconsistent, ambiguous). It also warns that an LLM grader rates question quality too generously, and that a recovery can look correct without being earned. Credit should go to fixes in the plan, not to good-sounding questions.

findings.claim: A design with hidden information, run under Full, Hidden and Interaction settings, can measure how much a dialogue with an informed simulated party recovers. Claude models recovered up to 80–89% of full-information performance, but models almost never ask unless explicitly prompted.
findings.source: Vijayvargiya et al., 'Interactive Agents to Overcome Ambiguity in Software Engineering' (Ambig-SWE), ICLR 2026, arXiv 2502.13069v3
findings.evidence: Underspecified issues are GPT-4o summaries of SWE-bench Verified issues. The settings are Full (the complete issue), Hidden (the summary, no interaction) and Interaction (the summary plus a GPT-4o user proxy that holds the full issue and answers "I don't have that information" for anything absent). Interaction recovers "up to 80%" of Full performance for Claude Sonnet 3.5 and Haiku 3.5, against 59% for DeepSeek and 54% for Llama 3.1, and Claude Sonnet 4 reaches 89%. "Without explicit prompting, models almost never interact, even for severely underspecified inputs." The per-setting resolve rates are only in a figure that I could not read.
findings.relevance: This is a template for Junior-dev cases: the case author holds the full design, the input plan is degraded, and the Full arm is the ceiling. It also shows that eliciting behaviour depends on the prompt, so the junior's questioning prompt is a real design variable.

findings.claim: When an LLM plays the user, the choice of model changes measured outcomes by several points, and simulated users misjudge task difficulty compared with real people.
findings.source: Seshadri et al., 2026, 'Lost in Simulation: LLM-Simulated Users are Unreliable Proxies for Human Users in Agentic Evaluations', ACL 2026, arXiv 2601.17087
findings.evidence: Abstract: "agent success rates varying up to 9 percentage points across different user LLMs". Simulated users were found "underestimating agent performance on challenging tasks and overestimating it on moderately difficult ones." They also introduce conversational artifacts and fail in different ways from human users. I read only the abstract.
findings.relevance: The junior is a simulated novice, so its model and prompt are factors in the experiment. Keep them fixed across arms. Run a sensitivity check with a second junior model, and occasionally compare against a human playing the junior, before attributing effects to the skill text.

findings.claim: Implementation by a fixed downstream executor discriminates between plan sources. Plan quality is a high-leverage factor, but the gain depends on the executor's capability band, and plan-based pipelines can cost almost as much as the strong model alone.
findings.source: Thangarajah, Chen, Hassan, 'DCAS', ASE 2026, arXiv 2608.06113; Gandhi et al., 2025, arXiv 2505.20182v1; Ning et al., 2024, 'Can LLMs Learn by Teaching for Better Reasoning? A Preliminary Study', NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2406.14629
findings.evidence: DCAS abstract (fetched): in a controlled plan-source intervention, "planning quality is a high-leverage component". The table values come through this repository's docs/research/planner-executor-split.md; the paper's HTML returned 404. With a Qwen3-Coder-30B executor on SWE-bench Verified: no plan 42.8, self-plan 48.2, Sonnet 4.5 plan 57.8, single run, n=500. Gandhi (Table 3, fetched): with o4-mini plans, GPT-4o-mini went from 0.1533 to 0.2933, against 0.4533 for the strong model alone. Total cost was $4.53, $29.68 and $33.33. With GPT-4o-mini plans and a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B executor, resolution stayed at 0.0467 and the valid-patch rate fell from 0.600 to 0.483. Ning (abstract, paraphrased by the fetch tool): teaching materials that are easier for students to learn tend to have clearer, more accurate logic, when the students learn in context.
findings.relevance: Having a pinned executor implement each arm's final plan against hidden tests is a valid confirmatory endpoint for plan quality. It is less exposed to judge bias. The executor and cases must sit in its headroom band, or plan differences will not show.

findings.claim: A reviewer's verdict changes sharply with how the artifact is presented to it. Assurances that it is fine cause large drops in detection, and the drops are largest for cheap models.
findings.source: arXiv 2603.18740v1 (2026), a study of framing and confirmation bias in LLM vulnerability review (250 CVE vulnerability–patch pairs, five framing conditions; authors reported by search as Mitropoulos et al., not verified)
findings.evidence: The conditions run from Neutral through Weak and Strong Bug to Weak and Strong Bug-free. Detection on vulnerable files, Neutral against Strong Bug-free: GPT-4o-mini 97.2% → 3.6%; Claude 3.5 Haiku 68.4% → 8.5%; DeepSeek V3 96.8% → 53.8%; Gemini 2.0 Flash 95.5% → 79.4%. "Bias effects are strongly asymmetric: false negative bias consistently exceeds false positive bias across all models." Strong Bug framing raised false positives by only 0.8 to 13.6 pp.
findings.relevance: This bears on the context-isolation choice. A full-context junior would read the main agent's confident narrative and might ask fewer probing questions. Test plan-only against full-context as an explicit arm, and never pass the main agent's assurances of completeness to the junior.

findings.claim: Single LLMs find a minority to about half of the seeded or expert-identified gaps in a specification. Issues of necessity and correctness, the closest analogue of flaws in architectural logic, are almost always missed. An ensemble of models raises recall.
findings.source: 'Detecting and Repairing Incomplete Software Requirements with Multi-LLM Ensembles', ASE 2025 NIER track; 'Two Truths and A Lie? Benchmarking Off-the-Shelf LLMs for Requirements Quality Assessment', arXiv 2609.03230
findings.evidence: ASE NIER abstract: "In experiments on four SRSs with seeded omissions, single models achieved only 0–52% recall," while the full ensemble "consistently exceeded 75% (up to 100%) recall with 95–100% suggestion plausibility." The 2609.03230 abstract (10 OpenAI and Anthropic models, 100 runs): the best Anthropic model "detects a median of only 47% of expert-identified issues" while "false-flagging 11%". "necessity and correctness issues are almost always missed"; generational progress is "non-monotonic". I read only the abstracts, and the NIER paper is a short early-results paper.
findings.relevance: Expect the junior's questions to cover seeded gaps only partially, especially logic and correctness gaps. Measure recall against the seeded ledger and false alarms separately. Running two independent juniors is a design variant worth testing.

findings.claim: Run-to-run noise in agentic evals is large compared with plausible effects, and naive standard errors understate uncertainty. Pairing, resampling and cluster-aware intervals are needed.
findings.source: Bjarnason, Silva, Monperrus, 2026, 'On Randomness in Agentic Evals', arXiv 2602.07150v1; Miller, 2024, 'Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations', arXiv 2411.00640
findings.evidence: Bjarnason: from 60,000 SWE-Bench-Verified trajectories, "single-run pass@1 estimates vary by 2.2 to 6.0 percentage points", with "standard deviations exceeding 1.5 percentage points even at temperature 0". "Detecting a 2% improvement at p<0.05 with 80% power requires approximately 9 runs per agent." Miller: "clustered standard errors can be over 3X larger than naive standard errors". With a score correlation of 0.5, paired differences "reduce the variance of the estimator by 1/3". Two answers per question cut variance by 1/3 and four by 1/2. Detecting a 3-point difference needs about 969 questions, and moving from 1 to 10 samples per question lowers the minimum detectable effect from 13.2% to 7.5%.
findings.relevance: With 12–20 cases, only large effects (about 15–20 pp in case-level strict success) are detectable. Treat the case as the cluster. Ledger items within a case are not independent. Use paired arms per case and 3–4 runs to cut within-case variance.

findings.claim: Iterating a prompt against a small dev set overfits it, and generic prompt additions can cause large regressions on some task types.
findings.source: Yang et al., 2024, 'Large Language Models as Optimizers' (OPRO), ICLR 2024, §5.4; arXiv 2601.22025, 'When Generic Prompt Improvements Hurt: Evaluation-Driven Iteration for LLM Applications'
findings.evidence: OPRO §5.4: "our training accuracies are often 5%-20% higher than our test accuracies"; "Setting aside a larger training set and optimizing for fewer steps (early stopping) may help reduce overfitting." 2601.22025 abstract: "generic prompt additions do not produce monotonic improvements". The largest decline was Qwen 2.5 on RAG, from 26/30 to 9/30 passing cases, "when generic rules are appended to the user prompt"; the suites had 30 cases each.
findings.relevance: A hill-climb on the Junior-dev skill text needs a held-out case set, early stopping, and guard metrics such as churn on null cases, unsupported claims and cost. Otherwise wording tuned to the dev cases will look like progress.

findings.claim: In this repository's own experiments, adding a review-and-revise loop to Haiku cost about 3.6 times as much per passing step and did not improve results. The instruments often failed to separate arms, and the skill rarely loads on its own.
findings.source: Repository: docs/evaluation/pilot-report-2026-11-08.md; evaluation/hygiene/README.md; plugins/code-comments/evals/README.md
findings.evidence: Pilot: the haiku-review arm (Sonnet review, then Haiku revise) passed 6/12 against 7/12 for haiku-plain. Cost per passing step was $0.281 against $0.077, and $0.321 for Sonnet-plain. "Adding a Sonnet review to Haiku cost almost as much as Sonnet and did no better." "Only 1 of the 6 steps separated the arms." Hygiene eval: "Five cases are too easy"; "Two or three runs per configuration per case can show a large effect, not a small one." Activation evals: Haiku loaded the skill in 0 of 18 should-load runs, Sonnet in 3 of 18.
findings.relevance: This is direct local precedent that review loops can add cost without a downstream gain, and that cases without headroom hide effects. Junior-dev needs a cost gate, cases chosen for headroom, and a separate eval of whether it triggers, because a loaded-on-instruction result does not show real-world use.

design_implications: Primary endpoint, a hidden gap ledger on seeded-gap cases (f4, f7, f8, f12). For each case, write a correct reference plan or Mermaid diagram and a private ledger of 8–15 load-bearing details: components, data flows, ordering, interface contracts, failure and rollback paths, and which layer owns each responsibility. Build the input by deleting or corrupting 2–4 ledger items in HumanEvalComm-style categories (incomplete, inconsistent, ambiguous) plus architectural ones (wrong layer, missing data path, missing failure mode). Score each ledger item as closed correctly, closed wrongly, or untouched. Report item recall (micro) and strict all-seeded-gaps-closed-with-no-regression (macro), as TravelPlanner does.

Include null and natural cases (f6, f13, f15). Null cases are complete, correct plans, where the right outcome is little or no change. They measure churn, regressions, harm caused by questions, and length inflation. Natural cases have the Haiku or Sonnet main agent write its own plan from a task with a ledger fixed in advance. They show whether real plans from those models have headroom, so the effect is not shown only on gaps the case author planted. Drop or redesign cases that do not separate the arms, as the hygiene eval had to.

Arms (f5, f11, f8, f6). A0: no review. A1: same-budget self-review, matched to the Junior-dev loop in tokens and rounds ('reread your plan as a newcomer would and revise it'). A1b: a one-pass instruction ('write this plan so a junior developer new to this stack could follow every step'), which tests Huang's point that feedback folded into the first instruction may suffice. A2: a generic critic subagent, plan-only, asked to list problems; A3, an adversarial reviewer, can wait. A4: Junior-dev, plan-only (the treatment). A5: Junior-dev with full context (repo plus conversation), which tests the isolation choice. A6: an oracle ceiling where the main agent is told which ledger items are missing. The decisive contrasts are A4 against A1 and A1b, and A4 against A5. A4 against A0 alone cannot support the claim.

Grading mechanics (f1, f2, f3, f4). Check mechanically wherever possible: Mermaid parses, required nodes and edges are present, named interfaces and components appear. For prose ledger items, use isolated binary judges, one per item, from a non-Claude family or a cross-family ensemble. Judges are blinded to arm, and the Q&A transcripts and any 'Junior asked…' sections are stripped before grading. Never let the main agent's model be the sole judge. Calibrate against at least 50 human-labelled items per case family and report kappa per arm. Use pairwise holistic preference only as a secondary metric, in both orders, counting a win only when both orders agree. Always record plan length and report a length-adjusted estimate.

Grader pre-flight before any paid run, following the repository's grade.py --self-test convention (f2, f4, f7). The reference plan must pass every ledger item. The seeded input must fail exactly the seeded items. A padded variant that adds words but no information must not gain. A plan that answers questions in conversation but never updates the artifact must get no credit.

Mechanism logging (f6, f7, f12). For each seeded gap, log whether any junior question targeted it (hit rate), whether the main agent's answer was correct, and whether the artifact changed accordingly (fix rate after a hit). Also log false alarms that led to harmful edits, and premature stopping: the junior declaring it understands while ledger gaps remain. This shows whether a failure lies in the junior's questions, in the main agent's answers, or in the decision to revise.

Downstream confirmation on a subset (f10, f13). Have a pinned executor (for example Haiku, with no access to the conversation) implement each arm's final plan in a fixture repo graded by hidden tests. Choose cases where the executor's baseline success is about 25–75%, as capability-gradient.md recommends. Make this the confirmatory endpoint, and use the ledger score as the cheaper development proxy. Report both, because a plan can satisfy the ledger and still fail to transfer.

Model factors (f9, f15). Cross the main agent across Haiku and Sonnet, and Opus as a ceiling if the budget allows, since the user's claim is about weaker models. Keep the junior's model and prompt fixed across arms. Run one sensitivity check with a second junior model, because the choice of simulated user moved outcomes by up to 9 pp. Report the per-tier effect descriptively; the interaction between skill and tier needs far more cases than a pilot.

Framing hygiene in the skill itself (f11). Give the junior only the artifact. Strip the main agent's assurances ('this plan is complete and correct') and its rationale summaries, because 'it is fine' framing cut a cheap model's detection from 68% to 9%. If A5 (full context) is not better than A4, that supports keeping the junior isolated.

Sample size and analysis (f13, f15). Pilot with 12–20 cases (4–6 per seeded category plus nulls) × 3 runs × 5–6 arms × 2 main-agent models. Each session is a multi-turn loop, so price a smoke run first. Average within each case and arm, compare arms paired by case, and use a cluster bootstrap over cases. Do not treat ledger items as independent trials. Expect to detect only effects of about 15–20 pp in case-level strict success. Predeclare the primary contrast (A4 minus A1) and a practical margin.

Cost gate (f5, f10, f15). Log tokens and dollars for junior questions, main-agent answers and revisions. Report cost per ledger gap closed and per downstream pass. Predeclare that Junior-dev must beat A1 by the chosen margin at no more than an agreed cost multiple, given the local pilot where a review loop cost $0.281 against $0.077 per passing step with no gain.

Hill-climbing loop for the skill text (f14, f4, f15). Split cases into dev and held-out sets (about 60/40) by case family. Change one thing per iteration. Run the dev set with 3 runs per arm and read every transcript. Accept a change only if A4 minus A1 improves on the primary metric with no regression on the guards: churn on null cases, unsupported claims, length inflation, cost, and no rise in premature 'understood'. Stop early when the dev score plateaus. Touch the held-out set only at milestones and refresh it once used. Track triggering in a separate activation eval, as the repository already does for code-comments.
open_questions: Does Junior-dev beat a token-matched self-review, or a one-pass 'write it for a junior' instruction, for Haiku and Sonnet main agents? No source tests a novice-explainee loop against these controls.

Do gains in ledger recall on seeded gaps transfer to plans the main agent writes itself, and to downstream implementation success? Planted gaps may be easier to surface than a model's own blind spots.

Is plan-only isolation better than a junior with full context? The framing-bias evidence comes from security review, not plan explanation, and a context-free junior may ask only about surface vocabulary.

Does the junior's 'I understand now' stop signal correlate with the ledger actually being complete, or does an LLM novice declare understanding too early, given that simulated users mis-calibrate difficulty?

How large is verbosity bias in current-generation judges? CALM shows modest robustness gaps. A withdrawn 2026 arXiv paper (2606.19544) claimed verbosity bias below 0.011 across 21 judges. This needs measuring on our own plan pairs before any holistic metric is trusted.
How should hidden ledgers be written so they do not echo the skill's preferred wording? The protocol requires independent authorship. Who writes the ledgers, and how is their completeness checked?

Which junior model gives the most useful questions? A weaker junior may ask about more basics; a stronger one may probe logic. Should Junior-dev run two juniors, given that ensemble recall beat single models in the requirements studies?

Can the main agent's answers in conversation that never reach the artifact be detected and penalised reliably? And how much do partially correct answers to the junior introduce new errors into the plan?

Will the skill trigger on its own when a plan or diagram is created? The existing code-comments skill loaded in 0 of 18 Haiku should-load runs and 3 of 18 Sonnet runs, so a loaded-on-instruction result may not reflect real use.

r.summary: Claude Code can make Junior-dev run without the user asking, but a skill description alone is not reliable for this. Plugin hooks are the deterministic route. The docs support a plugin layout with hooks/hooks.json (a Stop gate, or a PostToolUse nudge fed by a marker file) plus agents/junior-dev.md with a per-invocation model override. Multi-round dialogue is possible by resuming one subagent with SendMessage (retains full history) or by starting a fresh subagent per round with the transcript; SendMessage availability under claude -p is not confirmed. The local eval is the strongest evidence about activation: Haiku loaded the code-comments skill in 0 of 18 runs, and Vercel reports the skill was never invoked in 56% of cases. Public docs for claude plugin eval exist at code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals.md (fetched), contrary to the embedded note that none exists; the docs-map path /docs/en/plugins/plugin-evals.md returns 404. None of the mechanics research tests whether the junior improves plans; that remains unevidenced.

findings.claim: Plugin hooks fire on their events whether or not any plugin skill is invoked, so a hook is the only documented way to make a rule hold every time.
findings.source: Claude Code docs, 'Add components to a plugin' (plugins/components)
findings.evidence: "A plugin's hooks don't wait for one of the plugin's skills or commands to be used. Claude Code registers them when a session loads the plugin, and they fire on their events from then on." Also: "If a rule must hold every time, such as blocking edits to protected files, add it to the plugin as a hook rather than a skill." Plugin hooks live in hooks/hooks.json at the plugin root, same shape as settings.json hooks, e.g. {"hooks":{"PostToolUse":[{"matcher":"Write|Edit","hooks":[{"type":"command","command":"\"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/format.sh\""}]}]}}.
findings.relevance: Auto-running Junior-dev on plan/diagram files needs a hook, not a description match. Hooks ship inside the plugin.

findings.claim: Skill auto-loading is decided by the skill's description (plus when_to_use), which is capped in the listing and costs context on every turn.
findings.source: Claude Code docs, 'Extend Claude with skills' (skills)
findings.evidence: "Claude uses skills when relevant, or you can invoke one directly with /skill-name." "the description helps Claude decide when to load the skill automatically." "Put the key use case first: the combined description and when_to_use text is truncated at 1,536 characters in the skill listing." "Every skill in the skill listing adds to your context on every turn, whether or not Claude ever uses it." disable-model-invocation: true prevents automatic loading.
findings.relevance: Describes the mechanism only. It gives no activation rate, so a description-only trigger is unproven. The key use case must come first within 1,536 characters.

findings.claim: In this repository's own headless measurement, the code-comments skill almost never loaded on its own: Haiku loaded it in 0 of 18 runs, Sonnet in 3 of 18, while staying out of 12 of 12 non-trigger runs for both.
findings.source: Local file plugins/code-comments/evals/README.md (results 2026-11-09, Claude Code 2.1.319, 3 runs per case, with-arm only)
findings.evidence: "| Haiku | 0 of 18 runs | 12 of 12 runs | 30 of 30 | $0.07 |" "| Sonnet | 3 of 18 runs | 12 of 12 runs | 30 of 30 | $0.99 |" "The skill almost never loads on its own. Haiku never loaded it. Sonnet loaded it only for the request that is about comments (load-comment-refresh, three of three)" Caveats recorded in the file: three runs per case, one tiny repository, Bash not allowed, competing built-in and user skills present.
findings.relevance: The most direct evidence that a description-only trigger fails for Haiku. Junior-dev would be the main-agent-side trigger for Haiku, so this is the case to design around.

findings.claim: Independent vendor evaluation: a skill that is available but not told to be used is often never invoked; explicit instructions raised the trigger rate sharply, but results were sensitive to wording.
findings.source: Vercel, 'AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals' (Jan 2026 per secondary coverage)
findings.evidence: "In 56% of eval cases, the skill was never invoked." Table: "Baseline (no docs) | 53%", "Skill (default behavior) | 53% | +0pp", with explicit instructions "skills maxed out at 79% even with explicit instructions telling the agent to use them." An instruction added to AGENTS.md "improved the trigger rate to 95%+ and boosted the pass rate to 79%." "If small wording tweaks produce large behavioral swings, the approach feels brittle for production use." Number of evals, runs and model were not stated in the text I read; focus was Next.js 16 APIs.
findings.relevance: Supports the local finding that description-only triggering is unreliable. It also suggests an explicit, always-loaded instruction (for example in CLAUDE.md or a hook) raises invocation, and that Junior-dev trigger wording needs repeated testing.

findings.claim: PostToolUse runs after Write or Edit has already happened, so it cannot block the write. It can add context next to the result, or feed a reason back to Claude when continueOnBlock is set. The hook gets tool_input.file_path on stdin.
findings.source: Claude Code docs, 'Hooks reference' (hooks)
findings.evidence: Matcher example "Edit|Write" with "Edit\|Write and Edit, Write each match either tool exactly". Exit-code table: PostToolUse "No" can block, "Shows stderr to Claude; the tool already ran". "decision: \"block\" adds the reason next to the tool result. Claude still sees the original output; to replace it, use updatedToolOutput". "PostToolUse: by default the turn ends and the reason appears in the chat as a warning line. Set continueOnBlock: true to feed the reason back to Claude and continue the turn instead." Example reads FILE_PATH=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty') and prints {"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"PostToolUse","additionalContext":"..."}}.
findings.relevance: A per-edit PostToolUse detector can read the path and nudge Claude (additionalContext). A hard requirement needs continueOnBlock: true, otherwise the turn ends.

findings.claim: Stop and SubagentStop hooks can keep the agent working, with loop protections. The Stop input does not list which files were edited, so a gate must track edits itself.
findings.source: Claude Code docs, 'Hooks reference', Stop and SubagentStop sections (hooks)
findings.evidence: "Stop and SubagentStop hooks can control whether Claude continues." "decision: \"block\" prevents Claude from stopping"; "reason: Required when decision is block". "Claude Code applies an 8-consecutive-continuation cap"; override via CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP. "stop_hook_active ... is true when Claude Code is already continuing as a result of a stop hook." Stop input contains last_assistant_message, background_tasks, session_crons. "Does not run if the stoppage occurred due to a user interrupt." SubagentStop: "Returning decision: \"block\" with a reason keeps the subagent running and delivers reason to the subagent as its next instruction."
findings.relevance: A once-per-turn gate can see the finished plan. It needs a marker written by a PostToolUse hook to know a plan or diagram file changed, since Stop input does not list edited files. Guard against loops with stop_hook_active and a per-plan marker.

findings.claim: Two details needed for a file-detection hook could not be confirmed from the docs read: whether MultiEdit is still a matchable tool, and the exact tool_input field names for Write and Edit (content, new_string).
findings.source: Claude Code docs, 'Hooks reference' (hooks), read in several portions
findings.evidence: The matcher examples read only ever show "Edit|Write" or "Write|Edit"; the portion read states "The excerpt does not mention MultiEdit." The PostToolUse input-schema section was not in the portions returned, and the only tool_input field shown is file_path. The hooks debug log format is documented: "a PostToolUse hook on Write whose command prints hook-ran produces entries like: ... Hook PostToolUse:Write (PostToolUse) success:".
findings.relevance: Do not rely on a MultiEdit matcher. Confirm the Write/Edit input fields with --debug logs or a probe hook before building content detection on them.

findings.claim: A plugin can ship a subagent in agents/<name>.md. Its frontmatter sets tools and model. Omitting tools gives every subagent tool. The per-invocation model parameter overrides the frontmatter model. Plugin agents ignore hooks, mcpServers, permissionMode and initialPrompt.
findings.source: Claude Code docs, 'Subagents' (sub-agents) and 'Add components to a plugin, Agents' (plugins/components)
findings.evidence: "tools (optional): Tools the subagent can use ... Inherits every tool available to subagents if omitted." "model (optional): Model to use: sonnet, opus, haiku, fable, a full model ID such as claude-opus-5-5, or inherit." Resolution order: "(1) the per-invocation model parameter, (2) the frontmatter model ... (3) CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL, and (4) the main conversation's model." Plugin: "Ignored fields: permissionMode, hooks, mcpServers, and initialPrompt." Example file: agents/security-reviewer.md with name, description, model: sonnet; invoked as @agent-my-plugin:security-reviewer.
findings.relevance: agents/junior-dev.md with model: haiku or sonnet, plus a per-invocation override, lets the junior's model be swept separately from the main agent's. Tools must be set explicitly, or the junior inherits repo-reading tools and breaks its premise.

findings.claim: Each subagent invocation normally starts a new instance. A subagent can instead be resumed with SendMessage, and it then keeps its full prior history. Explore and Plan are one-shot and cannot be resumed.
findings.source: Claude Code docs, 'Subagents', Resume subagents (sub-agents)
findings.evidence: "Each subagent invocation creates a new instance rather than continuing an earlier one." "Resumed subagents retain their full conversation history, including all previous tool calls, results, and reasoning." "Claude uses the SendMessage tool with the agent's ID or name as the to field to resume it." "The built-in Explore and Plan agents are one-shot and return no agent ID." After a restart a name works only if it was set since the last compaction; an agent ID always works (v2.1.299 note). Availability of SendMessage under claude -p is not stated in the text read.
findings.relevance: Resuming one junior keeps its own earlier questions in context (fewer repeats across rounds). Starting fresh per round with the transcript is more reproducible and easier to evaluate. Both keep the junior away from the repo, if tools are restricted.

findings.claim: Headless claude -p and --bare change which hooks and plugins run. Under --bare, plugin hooks loaded with a flag do not run. Without --bare, -p runs project hooks. Stream output identifies subagent messages and loaded plugins.
findings.source: Claude Code docs, 'Run Claude Code programmatically' (headless)
findings.evidence: "--bare ... skipping auto-discovery of hooks, skills, custom commands, subagents, installed plugins ..." "Hooks still don't run in bare mode when you pass them with --settings, or in the hooks/hooks.json or hooks manifest key of a plugin you load with a flag. Don't use bare mode for a run that needs them." Load a plugin with "--plugin-dir <path>"; custom agents with "--agents <file-or-json>". "Messages from subagents ... appear in the stream as assistant and user messages. Their parent_tool_use_id field says which run each one belongs to." system/init reports "plugins" and "plugin_errors" for CI gating. Example: claude -p "..." --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages.
findings.relevance: Do not use --bare when testing hook-based triggers. Use stream-json with parent_tool_use_id to attribute junior-dev messages, and fail CI on plugin_errors.

findings.claim: claude plugin eval is documented publicly. It runs a plugin's eval cases in fresh sessions, with and without the plugin, and reports WITH, W/OUT and delta. The docs say the most common first failure is a Skill grader failing, meaning the description does not trigger on natural phrasing.
findings.source: Claude Code docs, 'Test plugins with evals' (plugin-evals)
findings.evidence: "The claude plugin eval shell command runs your plugin against a suite of test cases and scores the results." "each case runs three times by default." "WITH is the case's score with your plugin loaded, W/OUT is the score without it, and a positive Δ means the plugin raised the score." "The most common first finding is a Δ near zero with the case's tool_used: Skill grader failing, which means Claude isn't choosing your skill on natural phrasing." Layout: evals/<case>/prompt.md plus graders/*.md; example grader type: tool_used with tool: Skill and input_match '"skill"\s*:\s*"(?:[\w-]+:)?your-skill-name"'. Requirements: "Claude Code v2.1.269 or later." Commands: claude plugin eval . --allow-tools Write Edit; --json; --max-cost-usd; exit codes 0/1/2. Troubleshooting: "plugin eval is currently unavailable" means switched off server-side. Plugin hooks are loaded in runs: "loads the target plugin's skills, hooks, and agents".
findings.relevance: This is the harness for Junior-dev activation and quality checks. Note the embedded reference said no public page exists; this page exists at the URL given (fetched). The docs-map URL /docs/en/plugins/plugin-evals.md returned 404.

findings.claim: In plugin eval, Skill-invocation graders are excluded from the score in both arms unless marked arm: both. The Agent tool is in the default allowed set, but Write, Edit and Bash need --allow-tools.
findings.source: Claude Code docs, 'Test plugins with evals', 'Score against the no-plugin baseline' and 'Grant tools' (plugin-evals)
findings.evidence: "Every tool_used grader whose tool is Skill" is reported as indicator only; "arm: both ... for a 'must not invoke the skill' check with min: 0 and max: 0". "--ablation none: nothing is excluded." Read-only set: "Read, Glob, Grep, NotebookRead, Skill, AskUserQuestion, Agent, TodoWrite" plus task tools; "To let cases use Bash, Write, Edit, WebFetch, or WebSearch, grant them yourself: claude plugin eval . --allow-tools Write Edit \"Bash(npm test *)\"". Sandbox: the plugin's "skills, hooks, and agents" load; "Nothing personal or project-level loads".
findings.relevance: For Junior-dev, a Skill grader will not count. Use a tool_used grader on the Agent tool that names the junior (input key not yet confirmed), with arm: both or --ablation none, since the no-plugin arm has no junior.

findings.claim: The skill-creator workflow for description optimisation uses a split of 20 queries into train and test, with 3 runs per query and up to 5 iterations. It does not define a formal trigger-accuracy metric.
findings.source: anthropics/skills, skills/skill-creator/SKILL.md (GitHub raw)
findings.evidence: "Create 20 eval queries — a mix of should-trigger and should-not-trigger." (8–10 of each). "It splits the eval set into 60% train and 40% held-out test." "running each query 3 times to get a reliable trigger rate." "iterating up to 5 times". "selected by test score rather than train score to avoid overfitting." Triggering accuracy: "The source does not define a single triggering-accuracy metric or formula." Fetched text was model-summarised, so exact wording is approximate.
findings.relevance: A usable recipe for tuning the junior's trigger description: held-out queries that should and should not fire, repeated runs. It has no reported effect size.

findings.claim: Command hooks default to a 600-second timeout, prompt hooks to 30 seconds and agent hooks to 60 seconds. Async command hooks are not timed out, and asyncRewake can wake Claude when they exit with code 2.
findings.source: Claude Code docs, 'Hooks reference', common fields and asyncRewake (hooks)
findings.evidence: "Defaults: 600 for command, http, and mcp_tool; 30 for prompt; 60 for agent." "Claude Code doesn't enforce it on a command hook you run with async: true." asyncRewake: "wakes Claude on exit code 2", and its stderr, or stdout if stderr is empty, "is shown to Claude as a system reminder". The asyncRewake detail was read only partly.
findings.relevance: A PostToolUse hook could start a background junior run and wake the main agent when questions are ready, without blocking. Unverified for this use, so prototype it.

findings.claim: A forked skill, and a subagent started from a skill with context: fork, does not see the conversation. Its instructions must stand alone, and a guideline-only skill with no task returns nothing useful.
findings.source: Claude Code docs, 'Extend Claude with skills', Run skills in a subagent (skills)
findings.evidence: "Claude Code starts a new subagent of the type set in the agent field and gives it the skill content as its prompt. The subagent doesn't see your conversation history, so the skill's instructions have to stand on their own." "context: fork only makes sense for skills with explicit instructions. If your skill contains guidelines like 'use these API conventions' without a task, the subagent receives the guidelines but no actionable prompt, and returns without meaningful output."
findings.relevance: Junior-dev should be an agent with an explicit task prompt, not a guidelines-only skill run with context: fork. Its isolation from the conversation is then built in.

design_implications: Do not rely on the skill description alone to start Junior-dev automatically. The local eval shows Haiku at 0 of 18 recall (f3) and Vercel reports 56% never invoked (f4). Put the trigger in a plugin hook (f1), and keep the description as a secondary trigger with the key use case first and under 1,536 characters (f2).

Choose the trigger event carefully. A Stop hook gate runs once per turn, sees the finished plan, and can use decision or additionalContext with stop_hook_active and the 8-continuation cap (f6). Because Stop input does not list edited files (f6), pair it with a PostToolUse(Write|Edit) hook that records plan or diagram paths into a marker file (f5). Use a per-plan marker to avoid re-triggering. This is a design proposal, not a documented pattern.

For per-edit detection, parse tool_input.file_path with jq as the docs example does (f5). Use path patterns and fenced-block checks (mermaid fences, plan headings). Use additionalContext for a soft nudge. Use decision with continueOnBlock: true only where the junior must run, because a plain PostToolUse block ends the turn (f5).
Do not use a MultiEdit matcher, and confirm the Write and Edit tool_input field names with a probe hook and --debug logs before building content detection (f7).

Ship everything in the plugin: hooks/hooks.json at the plugin root and agents/junior-dev.md (f1, f8). Do not use --bare when testing triggers, because plugin hooks loaded with --plugin-dir do not run in bare mode (f10).

Define the junior as an agent with frontmatter name, description, model (haiku or sonnet) and an explicit tools list (f8). Pass the model per invocation to sweep the junior's model independently of the main agent's. Omitting tools gives every subagent tool, so an unrestricted junior could read the repo and break its premise (f8).

For the multi-round dialogue, either resume one junior with SendMessage, which keeps its earlier questions in context (f9), or start a fresh junior each round with the plan plus the Q&A transcript, which is easier to reproduce. Verify SendMessage works under claude -p before choosing resume (f9, f10). Either way, the junior should be an agent with a task prompt, not a guidelines-only context: fork skill (f15).

Evaluate with claude plugin eval (f11). Write cases for plan-creating prompts (should trigger) and non-plan prompts (should not). Grade activation with tool_used on the Agent tool, naming the junior in input_match. Do not rely on a Skill grader, which is excluded from the score unless arm: both (f12). Grant Write and Edit with --allow-tools (f12). Run --ablation none for activation, since the no-plugin arm has no junior (f12).
Trace the evaluation: run with --output-format stream-json --verbose, attribute junior messages with parent_tool_use_id, and fail CI on non-empty plugin_errors (f10).

Use more than the 3-run default for activation rates, because the local measurement (3 runs per case) was noisy and wording changes swing results (f3, f4). Borrow skill-creator's held-out train and test split and repeated runs for tuning the trigger wording (f13).

Check hook timeouts before putting the junior inside a hook. A command hook defaults to 600 seconds (f14). Consider an async hook with asyncRewake to run the junior in the background and wake the main agent with its questions (f14). This is unverified and needs a prototype.
open_questions: Is SendMessage available under claude -p, and does resuming work for a plugin-defined agent? The docs read do not say (f9, f10).
Can a subagent be given zero tools? The docs say omitting tools inherits all tools. They do not say whether an empty or deny-all list works, which matters for a junior with no repo access (f8).
What are the exact tool_input fields for Write (content) and Edit (old_string, new_string), and is MultiEdit still a tool name? Not confirmed in the portions read (f7).
Do plugin PostToolUse and Stop hooks actually fire inside claude plugin eval runs? The docs say the plugin's hooks load, but this was not tested (f11).
What is the input key for the Agent tool's subagent type (for example subagent_type), which an input_match grader needs? Not confirmed in the docs read (f12).

The docs page for claude plugin eval exists at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals.md, but the embedded reference said there was no public page. The version floor also differs (docs: v2.1.269; embedded reference: >= 2.1.198 for the command). Reconcile before citing either. Pin the Claude Code version in any experiment, since hook features like continueOnBlock and asyncRewake changed over recent releases (f11, f14).

None of the mechanics research tests whether a junior role-play improves plan or diagram quality, or whether it helps Haiku and Sonnet more than stronger models. That needs separate evidence (self-explanation, novice-explanation, and multi-agent review studies) and a controlled comparison of plans before and after junior rounds.

The Vercel post was read through a page-extraction tool. The 56% figure and the fragility statement are quoted from the extracted text. Its model, number of evals and runs were not stated in the text read, so treat it as weak evidence.

verdicts.note: Checked on PMC (Cognitive Science 26(5), 521-562; 12 studies). Study 2 self-ratings are 3.89, 3.10, 2.49 and 2.62 (they appear in Table 1, in the Study 5 section). The T1-T2 overconfidence values are in Table 7: devices .918, natural phenomena .860, narratives .351, facts .291, procedures -.173. For procedures the paper reports 'a slight (non-significant) increase', and for Study 1 the diagnostic question gave 'a further (non-significant) decrease'. Samples ran from 12 to 54 per study, mostly Yale students. The claim matches the source. In the non-device domains the task fitted the domain (naming a capital, telling a plot, listing steps) rather than giving a mechanistic explanation.

Read in the full Crawford & Ruscio text. The numbers are right: N = 306, 405 and 343. In the mechanistic condition, understanding fell 3.91 to 3.61 (1a) and 3.88 to 3.62 (1b). In the reasons condition it went 3.85 to 3.86 (1a) and 3.95 to 4.10 (1b). Partial eta squared was .31 in the original and .07 and .05 in the replications. Reasons increased extremity in both replications, and extremity, in-group favoritism and donations were unaffected. Two caveats. First, the measure is self-rated policy understanding, not confidence. Second, Crawford & Ruscio say Fernbach et al.'s own reasons-only analysis did find a drop in understanding after giving reasons. So 'reasons do not lower understanding' is a result of the replications that conflicts with part of the original. The evidence quotes Fernbach's abstract as if reasons had no effect at all, which is too broad.
verdicts.corrected_claim: In three preregistered replications, writing a mechanistic explanation reliably lowered self-rated policy understanding, by about 0.3 points on a 7-point scale (partial eta squared .07 and .05, against .31 originally). It did not moderate positions, in-group favoritism or donations. In the replications, listing reasons did not lower self-rated understanding (no change in one sample, a rise in the other) and made positions more extreme. Fernbach et al.'s original reasons-only analysis had, however, reported a decrease.

verdicts.note: Bisra et al. (Educ Psychol Rev 30, 703-725) is confirmed in the full text. It reports 69 effect sizes from 64 reports, N = 5,917, and g = .55 [.45, .65]. Self-explanation beat instructional explanation by g = .35 and no added explanation by .67. Justify prompts gave g = .42, longer-than-control studies .72 and equal-time studies .41, with the difference not significant. Conceptual beat metacognitive prompts (z = 3.284, p = .001). Chi 1994 is confirmed: 14 prompted vs 10 control eighth-graders, 2 h 5 min vs 1 h 6 min of study, and 'High explainers all achieved the correct mental model.' Problems: (a) Bisra defines 'metacognitive' prompts as asking learners to 'self-explain their planning or performance', not to 'rate your understanding'. There are only 3 such studies (N = 241). (b) The 'conceptualize' category means defining or elaborating a named concept (g = .87); the separate 'explain' category had g = .68. (c) 'Justify prompts are weaker' is a comparison of point estimates. Justify prompts were still significant, and no post-hoc test against conceptual prompts is reported. (d) 'The benefit depends on accurate self-monitoring' rests on Chi 1989, a correlational comparison of spontaneous Good and Poor students. It does not show that the prompting benefit depends on monitoring.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Self-explanation prompts improve learning outcomes (meta-analytic g = .55). In Chi et al. 1989, successful students' spontaneous self-explanations were associated with accurate self-monitoring, but this is not a tested condition for the prompting effect. Prompts to define or elaborate concepts (g = .87) did significantly better than metacognitive prompts to explain one's planning or performance (g = .19, n.s., k = 3). Justification prompts had a smaller but still significant effect (g = .42).

verdicts.note: The quotes and numbers are confirmed in the ASU PDF: the 'pervasive knowledge-telling bias' passage; 152 shallow vs 88 deep questions; deep responses 14% vs 41%; self-monitoring 21% vs 48%; Graesser & Person's 25 questions per hour, one third deep, '8 deep questions'; and the simulated-tutee suggestion. Scope problems: (a) the bias is shown for peer tutors, not for 'explainers' in general. (b) 'Only when they are deep' is too strong. Shallow questions also drew deep responses 14% of the time, and the review says only that 'in some circumstances, tutee questions can help to overcome the knowledge-telling bias.' (c) The question-response evidence comes from a single study (Roscoe & Chi 2004). 'Rare and mostly shallow' is supported (4-20% of behaviours; 'mainly shallow rather than deep').
verdicts.corrected_claim: Peer tutors show a pervasive knowledge-telling bias: even when trained, they deliver knowledge rather than develop it. In the one study that examined it, deep tutee questions were much more likely than shallow ones to draw deep responses (41% vs 14%) and self-monitoring (48% vs 21%). Tutee questions are infrequent and mostly shallow.

verdicts.note: Semantic Scholar API abstract (Learning and Instruction 74, 101438): Exp 1 (N = 147, laboratory) found no effect of explaining. In Exp 2 (N = 51, field, within-participants), only self-explaining beat the controls on transfer, and 'Self-explaining was more effective than instructional explaining.' The cumulative meta-analysis found a small effect of instructional explaining, moderated by modality (oral > written). The search-snippet number is partly right: the abstract gives g = 0.29 for conceptual knowledge and g = 0.22 for transfer. 'Mainly from oral explaining' is a fair reading of the moderation, but the abstract does not give a share.

OpenAlex abstract (JEP: Applied 5(2), 205-221): 'those with more expertise were worse predictors of novice performance times and were resistant to debiasing techniques'. It adds that intermediates 'may be more accurate'. The first sentence is supported, though the measure was predicted completion time for a novice task (a cell-phone task). The second sentence is the author's inference, which Hinds does not test. Hinds also points to intermediates, not novices, as the possibly more accurate predictors.
verdicts.corrected_claim: People with more expertise predicted novices' task-completion times worse, underestimating novice difficulty, and debiasing did not fix this. Intermediates may predict best. Whether adding a separate novice perspective helps is an untested inference from this result.

verdicts.note: Checked in the Microsoft Research PDF. Confirmed: 17 interviewees; 570 comments in 200 threads; surveys of 165 managers and 873 programmers; code improvements 165 (29%); defect fourth at 78 (14%), 'mostly address "micro" level and superficial concerns'; understanding 'the second most frequent category' ('clarification questions and doubts', plus the answers to them); understanding is the main challenge (from interviews); 798 (91%) and 716 (82%); 12 knowledge-transfer comments. Overstatement: 'Reviewers unfamiliar with the code mostly produce superficial comments and catch only obvious bugs' was not measured on comments. It rests on interviewees saying they 'look at "obvious bugs"' when the code is not theirs, and on 82% of survey respondents saying file owners give deeper feedback.
verdicts.corrected_claim: At Microsoft, interviewees named understanding the change as the main challenge of code review, and understanding (clarification questions and answers) was the second most frequent comment category. Defect comments were few (14%) and mostly micro-level. Interviewees and survey respondents reported that reviewers unfamiliar with the files look mainly for obvious bugs and give shallower feedback than file owners.

verdicts.note: Checked: the Shull 2000 abstract (unfamiliar domains; individuals and teams); the TR-225 text (the 'heuristics' / less-experienced passage; p = .143, .911, .063, .659; correlations under 14%; perspective ANOVAs p = .654, .945, .641); Ciolkowski 2009 on OpenAlex ('no clear positive effect'; teams 'less effective when compared to checklists'; 'researcher bias'); and the Regnell 2000 record (30 subjects; no significant difference in detection rate or defect coverage). Problems: (a) 'Does worse than checklists' applies to inspection teams on requirements documents in Ciolkowski's aggregation. The TR's individual comparisons mostly found PBR slightly better than checklists (not significant). (b) The TR ANOVAs test effectiveness and efficiency, not which defects are found. The TR's own defect-type analysis (RS3) found the perspectives 'appear to be complementary' for some documents. 'Do not find different defects' rests only on Regnell (one study, 30 students).
verdicts.corrected_claim: PBR improved defect detection in some early experiments, mainly with unfamiliar domains, and may suit less-experienced inspectors. Aggregated, it shows no clear advantage: PBR teams on requirements documents beat ad hoc reading but did worse than checklist teams, with signs of researcher bias. One experiment (Regnell et al. 2000, N = 30) found no significant difference in detection rate or defect coverage between perspectives. Other replications found partial complementarity.

verdicts.note: The Carver 2008 abstract on OpenAlex matches the evidence. I read the Albayrak & Carver replication in full (EMSE 19(1), 241-266, 2014; online 2012; 69 developers at three Turkish companies). The degree-field finding replicated, but with a redefined variable (amount of software-engineering content in the degree), and it was significant in two of three companies. The second sentence of the claim comes only from the original Microsoft study. The replication merged requirements, inspection and industrial experience and degree level into one 'Experience' variable, which significantly predicted effectiveness (F = 10.87, p = .002). The replication therefore does not back the idea that degree level and industrial experience do not matter.
verdicts.corrected_claim: At Microsoft, requirements inspectors with non-computing degrees found significantly more defects than those with computing degrees. A replication with 69 Turkish developers found software-engineering-heavy degrees were less effective (in two of three companies). In the original study, degree level and industrial experience did not matter but requirements-writing experience did. The replication could only test a combined experience measure, which mattered.

verdicts.note: The Votta 1993 abstract (OpenAlex) supports 'not as beneficial as managers and developers think' and 'cost much more'. I read Porter, Siy, Toman & Votta (IEEE TSE 23(6), 1997) in full. It cites Votta's industrial study of 50 design inspections at about 5% meeting gain and Humphrey at about 25%. Across its own 130 collection meetings (Lucent 5ESS code inspections), '30 percent of all defects discovered are meeting gains', and it calls the findings contradictory. The claim is supported. The evidence's secondary figure is wrong: 30% across 130 code inspection meetings, not 33% across more than 100.

The Sydney article (Elliot Varoy, republished from The Conversation) cites no direct study, traces the term to The Pragmatic Programmer, and argues from learning-by-teaching and self-explaining research. However, it links an experiment: Kurata, Tsuji & Fujinami (2024, IEEE GCCE), 'uh-huh duck'. That study tested an interactive duck against a plain one and reported better thought organization, so 'no direct empirical test' is too strong. 'No controlled test against a no-duck baseline' would be accurate. The Feynman meta-analysis (Dai et al., Advances in Education 16(9), 216-225, 2026, Hans) is confirmed: 41 studies, 44 effect sizes, N = 4,071, g = 0.468 [0.379, 0.556]. Its search terms included 'learning by teaching', 33 of 44 effect sizes measured declarative knowledge, and Egger's test gave t = 1.968, p = .056. The authors call this a moderate positive effect with no significant publication bias, so 'weak' is the auditor's appraisal of the evidence, not the source's finding. The paper calls university and STEM heterogeneity moderate (I² about 55-58%), not high. Feynman Bot: 14 participants over 3 days is confirmed.
verdicts.corrected_claim: No controlled study tests rubber-duck debugging against a no-duck baseline. Support is mainly anecdote plus analogy to self-explanation and learning-by-teaching, and one small study compared an interactive duck with a plain one. The only meta-analysis of the 'Feynman method' reports a moderate effect (g = 0.47). It is in a low-profile venue, has a borderline Egger test (p = .056), and defines the method through learning-by-teaching search terms, so the evidence is thin and conflated with learning-by-teaching.

verdicts.note: arXiv lists ICLR 2024, and Kamoi et al. is TACL 12:1417-1440 (2024). The quoted Kamoi findings are confirmed. The numbers are correct but come from Tables 3 and 4, not Table 1. Table 1 lists evaluation issues: oracle labels for RCI and Reflexion, an unfair comparison to self-consistency for Multi-Agent Debate, and sub-optimal prompt design for Self-Refine. So not all earlier gains are traced to oracle labels or external feedback. 'Weakest model degraded the most' is the auditor's inference, not the paper's. Llama-2 dropped most on GSM8K (-25.5) and on average. GPT-3.5 had the largest single drop (CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 in round 1, 41.8 in round 2), larger than Llama-2's on CommonSenseQA (-27.5).
verdicts.corrected_claim: Intrinsic self-correction (no external feedback) did not improve reasoning and often hurt it. Earlier reported gains came from oracle labels (RCI, Reflexion), unfair comparisons (multi-agent debate) or weak initial prompts (Self-Refine). The weakest model, Llama-2, lost the most on average, though GPT-3.5 had the largest single drop, on CommonSenseQA.
