verdicts.note: The quotes and numbers are confirmed on the arXiv HTML. Problems: (a) The large gains are not limited to preference and style tasks. Constrained Generation, scored automatically by concept coverage, rose 15.0 to 45.0 (+30). The low-gain tasks were Math (+0.2) and Code Optimization (+8.7). (b) The 94% 'everything looks good' figure is for ChatGPT on math only. It covers all instances, including ones already correct, so it should not be generalized to all 'tasks with hidden correctness errors'. (c) Vicuna-13B 'was not able to consistently generate the feedback in the required format'. The appendix reports a Vicuna-only math score (24.18%), rising to 40.5% when ChatGPT gave the feedback. 'Could not run the loop at all' overstates this.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Self-Refine's roughly 20% average gain comes mostly from preference-judged tasks and constrained generation. Correctness-focused tasks gained little (math +0.2, code optimization +8.7 for GPT-4). On math, ChatGPT's self-feedback said 'everything looks good' for 94% of instances, and Vicuna-13B could not reliably produce feedback in the required format.

verdicts.note: Confirmed on arXiv HTML (no venue listed): Blocksworld, GPT-4, 100 instances. Accuracy was 40% for the LLM alone, 55% for LLM+LLM backprompting and 88% for LLM+VAL. The LLM verifier approved 38 of 45 invalid plans (84.45%). Scope: Blocksworld is the only domain tested, so 'planning tasks' generalizes. 'More than doubles' is true but understates the gap: +48 points against +15, more than three times the gain.
verdicts.corrected_claim: In Blocksworld with GPT-4 (the only domain tested), the LLM verifier approved 84% of invalid plans. Backprompting with the sound external verifier VAL raised accuracy from 40% to 88% (+48 points), against 55% (+15 points) with LLM self-critique.

verdicts.note: Olausson et al. (Olausson, Inala, Wang, Gao, Solar-Lezama) appeared at ICLR 2024 (proceedings.iclr.cc). The conclusion quote, 52.60% vs 33.30% on 40 failing GPT-4 programs, the 1.58x factor, Table 2 overall APPS figures (Code Llama 1.1%, GPT-3.5 4.7%, GPT-4 10.8%) and 'Code Llama benefits less' all check out. Two caveats. First, the Table 2 figures count passing repairs divided by repairs sampled, not the share of failing programs fixed. Second, 'Code Llama benefits less' comes from the analysis by difficulty level, and the same appendix says the link between baseline strength and repair gains is unclear: GPT-3.5's introductory-level baseline resembles its HumanEval baseline, yet repair helps only on HumanEval. CRITIC (Gou et al., ICLR 2024) ChatGPT numbers match: AmbigNQ 74.9/67.3, HotpotQA 52.9/46.1 (Table 1) and GSM8K 78.2/77.0 (Table 2). The 'modest improvements or even deteriorate performance' quote is in the introduction. The GSM8K gap from tools is small (1.2 points).

All the numbers match. Spider: Codex 81.3->84.1, GPT-3.5 71.1->72.2, GPT-4 73.2->73.6, StarCoder 64.7->64.9. MBPP explanation deltas: +0.4, +2.0, -0.2, 0. The 'code execution plays an important role' conclusion is quoted correctly. Three overstatements. (1) The overconfidence quote reads 'both models tend to be overconfident' and refers only to GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (Sec 5.2.2 ablation on TransCoder/MBPP), not models in general. In the same no-execution ablation (Table 3), +Expl still gained about 3 points for Codex (TransCoder 80.4->83.9, MBPP 61.4->64.4) and for GPT-4 on MBPP (72.8->76.0). (2) Spider has no unit tests, but it is not execution-free: the paper executes the SQL and feeds the returned table into the explanation step. For GPT-3.5 and StarCoder, the whole Spider gain comes from simple feedback; explanation adds 0 on top. (3) The abstract presents Spider explanation gains as 'consistently improves the baseline by 2-3%' (9% on the hardest problems), which is more favourable than 'helps little'.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Self-explanation without unit-test execution gives small, uneven gains. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 tend to stay overconfident in their first answers (Codex and GPT-4 on MBPP still gain about 3 points). Adding explanation to unit-test feedback changes accuracy by -0.2 to +2.0 points, and by 0 for StarCoder. The authors conclude that code execution plays an important role in Self-Debugging.

verdicts.note: CoVe (Dhuliawala et al., Meta AI, arXiv 2309.11495) checks out. About 17% of baseline entities were correct vs about 70% answered correctly through individual verification questions. Llama 65B Wikidata precision went 0.17->0.36 (the 0.36 is the two-step variant). Biography FactScore went 55.9->71.4 (factor+revise). The 'should not attend to the original baseline response' quote is in Sec 4.3. Factored beat joint on every task: 0.32 vs 0.29, 0.22 vs 0.15, 0.48 vs 0.46, 63.7 vs 60.8. Qi et al. (arXiv 2305.14999) ChatGPT averages are 45.00 / 45.12 / 50.51 for Socratic (2 turns), at 9.22 calls per instance vs 1. For comparison, SC-CoT uses 20 calls and ToT 31.1. The sensitivity and overconfidence quotes are accurate.

Li, Kim & Wang (arXiv 2503.22674) is listed in the arXiv journal-ref as NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks. The abstract contains both quotes: '40-50% accuracy on Logic-Q and Planning-Q' and 'struggle to identify the right question even when they can solve the fully specified version'. The benchmark covers the case where exactly one necessary variable is missing. The task is choosing the right clarifying question from candidate options.

Ambig-SWE (Vijayvargiya, Zhou, Yerukola, Sap, Neubig) is listed as ICLR 2026 on mlanthology. 'up to 74%', 'almost never interact', the 89/80/59/54% figures, and 0.136 vs 0.135 with 39.6% vs 26.8% plus the 'integrate information' quote all match. However, the 89/80/59/54% are 'relative performance': the interaction resolve rate as a share of the Full-setting rate, not the share of the Hidden-to-Full gap recovered (the paper words this inconsistently). So 'recovers most of the lost performance' is not shown for DeepSeek-v2 or Llama 3.1 70B. Ask or Assume (Edwards & Schuster, EMNLP 2026 camera-ready) matches: 70.80 / 54.80 / UA-Single 61.20 / UA-Multi 69.40, $3.50 vs $2.03, GPT-5.1 simulator holding the full issue. The claim leaves out a key result: the paper's single-agent Interactive Baseline, prompted that the issue is incomplete so asking is compulsory, scored 70.40%. That is statistically indistinguishable from UA-Multi (p = 0.621) and cheaper ($1.40 per task). The multi-agent detector beats only the uncertainty-aware single agent that decides for itself whether to ask. Only two backbones were tested (Sonnet 4.5, Kimi K2.6).
verdicts.corrected_claim: On underspecified SWE-bench tasks, interaction lifts resolve rates to 54-89% of full-specification performance, depending on the model. Models almost never ask unless told to, and weaker models make worse use of the answers they get. Among agents that must decide for themselves whether to ask, a separate underspecification-detecting agent (69.4%) beats a single agent with an ask tool (61.2%), but costs more. A single agent told outright that the issue is incomplete does about as well (70.4%).

verdicts.note: ClarifyGPT (Mu, Shi, Wang, Yu, Zhang, Wang, Liu, Wang; arXiv 2310.10996; no venue on the arXiv page) abstract matches. Human evaluation with 10 participants on MBPP-sanitized: GPT-4 70.96%->80.80%. Simulated evaluation across four benchmarks: GPT-4 68.02%->75.75% (+7.73) and ChatGPT 58.55%->67.22% (+8.67). Ambiguity is detected 'by performing a code consistency check'. The gains are similar, as the claim says.

Khan et al. (arXiv 2402.06782v4) GPT-4-Turbo judges: naive 48%, consultancy 54%, debate 76% (75.6% in Insight 1), expert 92.5%. Human judges: 60% / 78% / 88%. Both quotes are accurate. Consultants argue the correct and incorrect answers equally often, and 'higher consultant skill' means best-of-N optimisation. 'Gains little accuracy' holds for LLM judges (+6 points) but not for human judges, where consultancy raised accuracy from 60% to 78% (+18). Kenton et al. (arXiv 2407.04622): 'debate outperforms consultancy across all tasks when the consultant is randomly assigned' is verified. The 'less frequently convinced by the wrong answer' result comes from the setting where debaters and consultants choose their own side. Kenton also reports that debate vs direct QA is mixed on tasks without information asymmetry.
verdicts.corrected_claim: In consultancy, where a judge who cannot see the source text hears a single expert, LLM judges gain little accuracy (48% -> 54%). Human judges gain more (60% -> 78%). Both are more easily misled by an incorrect expert, especially a more persuasive (best-of-N) one. Adversarial debate does better: 76% for LLM judges and 88% for human judges.

verdicts.note: Sharma et al. (arXiv 2310.13548, ICLR 2024): models admit mistakes on between 42% (GPT-4) and 98% (Claude 1.3) of questions and change answers on 32% to 86%. Accuracy drops 'by up to 27% (Claude 1.3)' in Sec 3.2. Sec 3.3 attributes a 27% figure to LLaMA 2, so the paper is internally inconsistent. The 'Swaying is not limited...' quote is accurate. Laban et al. (arXiv 2311.08596): 10 LLMs on 7 classification tasks, flipping 46% of the time on average, with an average 17% accuracy drop.

Turpin et al. abstract (comments field: NeurIPS 2023) matches. The example is reordering few-shot multiple-choice options so the answer is always '(A)'. Accuracy dropped 'by as much as 36%' on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks with GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0. The models 'systematically fail to mention' the biasing features, and explanations are 'plausible yet misleading'.

The content matches both abstracts: over-competency dominates, prescribed misconceptions are dropped or required steps skipped, the same trigger leaks more in multi-turn than in isolation, more capable models adhere better, and reasoning helps single-turn fidelity but is associated with more multi-turn leakage. Song, Guo & Lin (arXiv 2603.26142, no venue listed): prompt-only novices give 'expert-level explanations' and unlearned agents are more novice-like. Neither abstract gives numbers. The venue is overstated: 'Too smart for its own good?' (Xu, Beigman Klebanov, Mikeska) is a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop 'Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB)', not the main conference. It also studies simulations of young learners specifically.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Same claim, but cite the first source as Xu, Beigman Klebanov & Mikeska 2026, 'Too smart for its own good? Competence Leakage in LLM Simulations of Young Learners', NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpreting Agent Behavior (poster). Note that its evidence concerns simulated young learners.

verdicts.note: Ning et al. is NeurIPS 2024 (poster 96924). M1 figures on 181 MATH problems match: 91.71->96.69, 91.71->95.03, 81.77->87.85. The 'Strong teachers can improve even when teaching weaker students' quote and the 'clearer and more accurate logic' finding are accurate. The LbT score is the students' exam accuracy on similar problems, not self-report. Two caveats. (1) M1 is training-free answer selection: it picks the teacher's best answer using student exam scores and leaves the weights unchanged. So the strong-teacher results show better selected answers, not a teacher model that has learned. Weight updates come from M2 (DPO, LLaMA3-8B 29.0 -> 32.2 vs 30.4 for correctness-based DPO). (2) 'About 61->67 F1' for M3 mixes two conditions. Mixed students go 63.66 -> 67.09. LLaMA3-70B as the only student goes 61.08 -> 63.96 (peak 65.40).
verdicts.corrected_claim: Learning by teaching can improve a teacher LLM's outputs, including strong teachers teaching weaker students. Scoring the teacher's candidate answers by the students' measured exam performance, not their self-reports, raised MATH accuracy by 3-6 points over self-consistency. Using the same signal for DPO fine-tuning modestly improved a small model (29.0 -> 32.2).

verdicts.note: The core claim is supported. Du et al.: gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, 3 agents, 2 rounds, GSM8K 77.0 / 75.0 / 81.0 / 85.0; the 'not necessarily correct' and confident-affirmation passages are present. Choi et al. (NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight) quotes are accurate. Wang et al.'s 'almost the same performance' quote is accurate, though their multi-agent discussion does beat a single agent when the prompt has no demonstrations. Smit et al.'s quotes are accurate, but they also report that tuned MAD (Multi-Persona, agreement modulation) can 'surpass all other non-debate protocols'. Three citation problems. (1) The 'Huang Table 7' numbers (SC@9 88.2 vs debate 83.0) are correct, but they come from Huang et al. 2023, 'Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet' (arXiv 2310.01798), which is missing from the source list. (2) The Liang paraphrase is garbled: Degeneration-of-Thought afflicts self-reflection, while the 'adaptive break' is what MAD needs to work well. Liang (EMNLP 2024) is a pro-MAD paper. (3) Smit's positive caveat is left out.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Multi-agent debate gains are real in some setups, but most of them come from extra samples or majority voting. Self-consistency at matched sample counts beat debate in Huang et al. 2023 (88.2 vs 83.0). Debates often converge on confident wrong answers, and a single agent with strong prompts largely matches them when demonstrations are given. Add Huang et al. 2023 (arXiv 2310.01798) to the sources.

verdicts.note: Tyen et al. (Findings of ACL 2024) direct step-level mistake-finding figures match: GPT-4 52.87%, GPT-3.5-Turbo 14.78%, PaLM 2 Unicorn 23.67%. The oracle backtracking gains on originally incorrect traces match: +18.04 to +43.92, with tracking shuffled objects at +43.92 (random +20.39). Tsui's Self-Correction Bench (accepted to COLM 2026) matches: a 64.5% blind spot across 14 open-source non-reasoning models, cut 89.3% by appending 'Wait'. Scope is overstated. The backtracking experiment ran on one model only (PaLM 2 Unicorn). Random locations also gave +5 to +21 points. Oracle backtracking cut accuracy on originally correct traces by up to 11 points. Tsui's 'external' errors are errors in user-provided input, and the result covers only non-reasoning open models.
verdicts.corrected_claim: The bottleneck in self-correction is largely locating the error. Frontier models find mistakes in reasoning traces poorly (GPT-4 about 53%). Given the oracle error location, PaLM 2 recovered 18-44 points on incorrect traces, at some cost on correct ones. Open non-reasoning models correct errors presented as user input far more often than identical errors in their own output (64.5% blind spot).

verdicts.note: MAST (Cemri et al., arXiv 2503.13657v3) matches: 1,642 traces, 7 frameworks, human kappa 0.88. Every failure-mode percentage matches (FM-2.2 6.80%, FM-2.6 13.2%, FM-3.2 8.20%, FM-3.3 9.10%, FM-3.1 6.20%, FM-1.5 12.4%, FM-1.3 15.7%), as do the superficial-verifier quote and the 41%-86.7% failure range. Table 5 ChatDev ProgramDev-v0 reads 25.0 / 34.4 / 40.6, and Appendix H.2 says 'they do not constitute substantial improvements'. Caveats: clarification failure (6.8%) is one of the less frequent modes. In the AG2/GPT-4 case study, the improved prompt with a verification section 'significantly outperforms the baseline'. The authors say the interventions are 'not universal'.

Both sources exist as cited. R2ABench (arXiv 2604.06683) is by Minxiao Li, Li Zhang, Shuying Yan, Fang Liu, Liehao Li, Yang Liu and Xiaoli Lian: v1 8 Apr 2026, v3 9 Sep 2026, and v3 grows to 68 projects. In v1 the 17 PRDs, the Table 3 direct-generation Node F1 (0.5413–0.6699) and Edge F1 (0.0855–0.1760), the direct-generation orphan ratio (12.64–20.25%), the E1–E4 examples (Sonnet-4.6 reduces 20+ BLL nodes to 'five coarse-grained nodes'; GPT-5 adds a 'Log Aggregator with 12 associated log edges'), 'structurally fragmented architectures' and the agent instability all check out. Error: in Table 4 (macro average), removing the architecture section (-Arch) moves the orphan ratio from 15.96% to 19.28%. The 20.23% figure is the Min setting, which keeps only Core Objectives and Functional Features. The paper also defines E5 (render/syntax failures). Ferrari et al. check out: GPT-3.5 ChatGPT, 87 diagrams, kappa 0.67, completeness 3.63, correctness 3.22 (p=0.10, not significantly above 3), understandability 4.37, the '10 player statistics' and 'Study Results' examples, and the conflict 'hidden by the function call' 'Determine selected value'. The quoted phrase 'Inconsistent requirements were concealed' does not appear in v2; the closest wording is 'the inconsistency ... is not only hidden'. The claim itself is fair, though v3's abstract names edge hallucination and relation modeling, not node omission, as the main failure.
verdicts.corrected_claim: LLM-generated architecture and UML diagrams often omit or over-aggregate components, add components the requirements never mention, misplace layer boundaries and, above all, get relationships wrong; edge recovery is much weaker than component identification. Conflicts between requirements can hide behind vague function calls. (R2ABench v1 ablation: removing the architecture section raised the macro orphan ratio from 15.96% to 19.28%; the minimal-input setting reached 20.23%.)

verdicts.note: Confirmed against v3: Vijayvargiya, Zhou, Yerukola, Sap and Neubig; 500 SWE-bench Verified issues; a GPT-4o proxy that answers 'only using information explicitly present in it'; 'up to 74% over the non-interactive settings'; Sonnet 4 recovers about 89% of full-spec performance (Sonnet 3.5 and Haiku 3.5 up to about 80%, Deepseek-v2 59%, Llama 54%); 'Without explicit prompting, models almost never interact'. The detection accuracies are each model's best prompt in Table 2 (Sonnet 4 0.89 strong, Sonnet 3.5 0.84 moderate, Haiku 0.63, Llama 0.52, Qwen 3 Coder 0.50). Deepseek-v2 (best 0.69) was also tested. The paper says 'the models, except Claude Sonnet, fail to reliably distinguish them', and Sonnet 4 itself scores only 0.74 under a neutral prompt. The template, question-quality and prompt-engineering conclusions all match.

Confirmed: Wu and Fard, HumanEvalComm, ACM TOSEM, arXiv 2406.00215v3. The abstract's 'more than 60% ... still generate code' is there, as are the Communication Rates (ChatGPT 14.21%, DeepSeek Coder 30.76%, Okanagan on ChatGPT 72.73%), the Good Question Rates (13.43% to 52.24%), the 95% figure under 50% random removal, and Okanagan asking unnecessary questions on the original, complete problems. Small evidence caveat: the 35–52% Pass@1 figure is a relative drop, and the paper scopes it to 'the rest open-source models'. Its upper bound actually matches ChatGPT's drop in Table 3.

The empirical part checks out: Dhuliawala et al., Findings of ACL 2024 (2024.findings-acl.212), Llama 65B; Wikidata 0.17 / joint 0.29 / 2-step 0.36 / factored 0.32; MultiSpanQA 0.39 / 0.46 / 0.48; FactScore 55.9 / 60.8 / 63.7 / 71.4; and the rationale quote. The inference goes beyond the source. In CoVe the verification questions are planned from the draft, and only the answering step is cut off from it. The isolated answerer never sees the artifact under review at all, so the result is about not anchoring on the draft, not about a questioner who sees only the artifact. The tasks are closed-book fact recall (lists, QA, biographies), not code review. On Wikidata the best variant is 2-step, not factored.
verdicts.corrected_claim: In Chain-of-Verification (Llama 65B, fact-recall tasks), answering verification questions without the draft in context reduced hallucination more than answering them with the draft visible. By analogy, this suggests a checker should not be anchored on the author's own output or reasoning; it was not tested for code review or for a questioner who sees only the artifact.

verdicts.note: Checked against the extracted PDF text. Every number is right: Spider Table 2a Simple to +Expl (Codex 81.3 to 84.1, GPT-3.5 72.2 to 72.2, GPT-4 73.4 to 73.6), and Table 3 without unit-test execution (TransCoder 83.4/83.9, 89.1/89.1, 78.2/78.0; MBPP 57.6/64.4, 68.2/68.2, 76.0/76.0). The two quotations are verbatim. Problem: Spider is not an 'explanation without execution' setting. Section 4.1 says 'we execute the SQL query and add the returned table to the model input for code explanation'. Spider only lacks unit tests. The truly execution-free results are in Table 3, where Codex still gains up to about 5% (MBPP 61.4 baseline to 64.4 with Expl, 66.2 with Trace), GPT-4 gains 3.6 on MBPP, and GPT-3.5 gains about nothing. The paper calls the 2–3% Spider gain 'consistent' (for Codex across sample sizes), and its summary is that 'code execution plays an important role ... however, sometimes LLMs can still improve ... purely with self-generated feedback'. 'Most of the improvement comes from running the code' is supported: with unit tests, TransCoder Codex reaches 92.5 against 83.9 without.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Rubber-duck explanation helps modestly. On Spider, where there are no unit tests but the SQL is still executed and its returned rows shown, Codex gains about 3 points, and GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 gain about nothing. With no code execution at all, gains are small and vary by model (Codex up to about 5%, GPT-4 3.6% on MBPP, GPT-3.5 none). The largest gains (up to about 12%) come when unit-test execution feedback is available.

verdicts.note: Valmeekam, Marquez and Kambhampati (arXiv 2310.08118v1) are confirmed: GPT-4, 100 Blocksworld instances; LLM+LLM 55/100, LLM+VAL 88/100, generator only 40/100; the verifier's false positive rate is 38/45 (84.45%). Tyen et al. (Findings of ACL 2024, 2024.findings-acl.826) are confirmed: GPT-4 39.80/52.87/43.40 and GPT-3.5 10.44/14.78/14.31. Backtracking with PaLM 2 Unicorn gave Δ✗ +18.04 to +43.92 and Δ✓ −0.00 to −11.43, and a random location gave smaller gains. Two overstatements. (1) 'The same models fix errors well once shown where they are': correction given the location was tested only on PaLM 2 Unicorn, not GPT-4. Valmeekam found that the amount of feedback had 'minimal influence' (binary only 74% against 86% with the first error, n=50), so the problem there is unreliable verification, not missing location. (2) 'Revising steps that were already correct costs accuracy': Tyen's Δ✓ losses come from backtracking at a labeled mistake step in traces whose final answer was nonetheless correct ('despite the correct answer, there is a logical mistake in one of the steps'). Random-location backtracking, which may hit correct steps, cost −6.67 to −15.91 on those traces.
verdicts.corrected_claim: LLMs are poor at finding errors in their own plans and reasoning: a GPT-4 plan verifier judged 84% of invalid Blocksworld plans valid, and mistake-finding accuracy was at most about 53% (GPT-4). Given the true mistake location, PaLM 2 corrected many wrong-answer traces (+18 to +44 points). Revising traces that had already reached a correct answer cost accuracy (up to −11 points at the true location, up to −16 at random locations). A sound external verifier helps far more than the detail of its feedback.

verdicts.note: AgentVerse (Chen et al., ICLR 2024) is confirmed: for GPT-3.5-Turbo 'the Group setup underperforms the Solo setup in two of three tasks' (Creative Writing 93.6 to 92.3, MGSM 82.4 to 80.8), attributed to 'susceptibility to erroneous feedback'; the 'easily swayed' quote; 'Roughly 10% of errors in the MGSM dataset'; and 'this phenomenon is absent in GPT-4-based agents'. HumanEval Solo to Group is 74.4 to 75.6 and 87.2 to 89.0, with the unit-test agent stated for GPT-4. FlipFlop (Laban et al.) matches its abstract: ten LLMs, seven classification tasks, 46% average flip rate, 17% average accuracy drop. The first sentence generalizes one qualitative observation about one model (GPT-3.5-Turbo against GPT-4) to 'weaker models' in general. FlipFlop's challenge is a user's 'Are you sure?', not another agent's feedback.
verdicts.corrected_claim: In AgentVerse, GPT-3.5-Turbo agents were sometimes swayed from correct answers by another agent's incorrect feedback (about 10% of MGSM errors), while GPT-4 agents were not. Separately, challenging LLMs with 'Are you sure?' made them flip answers 46% of the time on average, with a 17% average accuracy drop across ten models.

verdicts.note: Both sources exist. Keramati, Cao, Mohammadi, Warschauer and Shi is in the EDM 2026 proceedings (short papers, pp. 532–540; arXiv 2606.14113). Song, Guo and Lin is arXiv 2603.26142. The quotes and numbers check out: Condition Logic 46.4% against 24.9%, Other 7.1% against 28.3%, five models including claude-sonnet-4 and gpt-5, and the Song paper's 'act like a novice' and 'prompt-based role assignment does not alter the model's underlying pre-trained knowledge' (Section 1). Caveats. The EDM 'general prompting ... near-perfect solutions' sentence is background citing prior work [30, 27], not a result of the paper. 'Idealized novice' describes errors that Claude Sonnet 4 (Self-Refine) produced when explicitly asked to write one logical error. Those errors were rated more plausible than real ones (4.27 against 3.78), 83.7% were labeled human-written, and the abstract calls them 'functionally indistinguishable', though they cluster on clean, single-purpose bugs. The Song paper's role-assignment statement is a motivating claim; it reports no prompt-only numbers.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Prompting an LLM to role-play a novice does not remove its expertise: 'act like a novice' prompts can still yield expert-level explanations (a motivating claim, not measured against prompt-only baselines). Even when explicitly asked to produce student-like errors, models produce cleaner, more stereotyped bugs than real students ('an idealized novice'; Condition Logic 46.4% against 24.9%), although expert annotators found them plausible and mostly could not tell them from student code.

verdicts.note: docs/research/planner-executor-split.md (R6, #36, 2026-11-07) supports each part. DCAS 42.8/48.2/57.8 and 'scales with planner capability' (line 42). Liu et al. 'a subpar plan hurts performance even more than no plan at all', with capable models overriding plans that do not fit (lines 63–66). RealBench Sonnet 4 17.5% to 6.2% and 'is insufficient without implementation details' (lines 80–83). Implementation holds real decisions (lines 26–28, 92–93). Hybrids keep a strong model or tests: 'Every hybrid that preserved quality had one or the other' (lines 188–190). R2 §2.4 cited (line 187). The README pilot note is at docs/research/README.md lines 79–80. Minor: the evidence's quotation is a paraphrase. The doc actually says 'Every quality-preserving hybrid kept the strong model active during or after execution' (line 157). The claimed findings are mostly cited from other papers, not R6's own measurements; the doc says no experiment was run.

Zheng, Pei, Logeswaran, Lee and Jurgens (Findings of EMNLP 2024; arXiv 2311.10054v3): 162 roles, 4 LLM families, 2,410 factual questions; 'adding personas in system prompts does not improve model performance'; 'the effect of each persona can be largely random'; 'automatically identifying the best persona is challenging'. Choi, Zhu and Li (NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight; arXiv 2508.17536v2): 'Majority Voting alone accounts for most of the performance gains typically attributed to MAD' across seven NLP benchmarks; debate 'induces a martingale over agents' belief trajectories, implying that debate alone does not improve expected correctness'. Scope caveats: the persona result covers objective factual QA only. Choi et al. also find that biasing debate toward correction can 'meaningfully enhance debate effectiveness'.

Zheng et al. (MT-Bench / Chatbot Arena, arXiv 2306.05685v4; NeurIPS 2023 Datasets & Benchmarks) checks out: Table 2 default consistency (Claude-v1 23.8%, GPT-3.5 46.2%, GPT-4 65.0%), 'Most LLM judges favor the first position', the Table 3 repetitive-list failure rates (91.3/91.3/8.7%), the self-enhancement win rates (10% and 25%) with the caveat that the authors 'cannot determine' a bias, the both-orders mitigation, few-shot 65.0 to 77.5%, and 85% GPT-4 agreement against 81% human-human (S2). CALM (Ye et al., ICLR 2025): the Table 7 default rows give position robustness 0.776 for GPT-4o and 0.832 for Claude-3.5, and verbosity 0.977 and 0.952. Table 5 gives self-enhancement error rates of 1.74 (GPT-4o) and 7.48 (Claude-3.5), and the anonymization quote is verbatim. Notes: the 'current' judges are 2024 models (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet-0620). Zheng calls the both-orders rule a 'conservative' approach; 'standard' is the auditor's own characterization.

Dubois, Galambosi, Liang and Hashimoto, arXiv 2404.04475 (listed as COLM 2024). Confirmed: 'AlpacaEval is highly length gameable'; gpt4_1106_preview's win rate 'fluctuates from 22.9% to 64.3%' under the verbosity prompts and 'only fluctuate[s] from 41.9% to 51.6%' with length control; normalized standard deviation 'decreases from 25% to 10%'; GLM conditioning 'with a zero difference in lengths'; Spearman correlation with Chatbot Arena from 0.94 to 0.98. The swing narrows from about 41 points to about 10. Note: the swing comes from prompting for different verbosity (one baseline model on AlpacaEval), which the paper attributes to length.

Pombal, Rei and Martins (arXiv 2604.06996, v3 3 Aug 2026): judges issue 'binary verdicts on individual evaluation criteria'; on IFEval and LiveCodeBench they are 'more than 50% more likely to incorrectly mark them as satisfied when the output is their own'; HealthBench is skewed 'by up to 10 points'; ensembling 'helps mitigate SPB, but without fully eliminating it'. Family bias is measured as a result of the paper, not just background (Section 3: 'Judges favor themselves and models from their family even with objective rubrics'; Table 5 family-level ratios), though the Llama family showed no strong family preference on HealthBench. Wataoka, Takahashi and Ri (arXiv 2410.21819; NeurIPS 2024 SafeGenAI workshop): 'GPT-4 exhibits a significant degree of self-preference bias'; LLMs rate lower-perplexity outputs higher than humans do 'regardless of whether the outputs were self-generated'.

The quotes and numbers check out. TICK (Cook, Rocktäschel, Foerster, Aumiller, Wang; arXiv 2410.03608, preprint with no venue): exact agreement 46.4% to 52.2% against direct scoring (GPT-4o judge, internal 612-instruction set, +5.8 points), and human inter-annotator agreement 0.194 to 0.256 ('still low, despite being improved'). TravelPlanner (Xie et al., ICML 2024 Spotlight): the 'pre-defined scripts', macro and Final Pass Rate definitions, and GPT-4 at 0.6%. The Anthropic guide (2026-01-09, vendor): all three quotes are verbatim, and it also lists 'binary (all graders must pass)' scoring. The problem is the synthesis. TICK's agreement gain was measured with a checklist pass rate equal to the fraction of YES answers, not a strict all-items pass. TravelPlanner's strict all-constraint rates are computed by programmatic scripts, and it reports no agreement with humans. No cited source shows that the strict all-items rate raises human agreement. The isolation of each item is recommended by the vendor guide and only implied by TICK's per-question template. Human calibration comes from the vendor guide; TICK reports question-level accuracy of 0.826 against majority human votes.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Decomposing grading into binary per-item checklist questions modestly raised LLM-judge agreement with human preferences (TICK: 46.4% to 52.2% exact agreement, with items scored as a fraction passed). Benchmarks such as TravelPlanner report a strict pass rate requiring every constraint, checked by scripts. Vendor guidance recommends isolated per-dimension LLM judges calibrated against human experts. None of these shows that the strict all-items rate itself improves human agreement.
